item.title: xFusion Tech Day – Bangladesh highlights AI-driven innovation, enterprise infrastructure and next-generation technology solutions
item.description:
xFusion International, in collaboration with Inflow Technologies, successfully hosted “xFusion Tech Day – Bangladesh” under the theme “Building the Agentic Era Together” on 29 October 2026 at La Vita Banquet Hall, Lakeshore Hotel, Gulshan, Dhaka, reports a press release.

The event brought together technology leaders, industry experts, business partners and enterprise professionals to explore emerging technology trends, enterprise infrastructure solutions and opportunities for digital transformation in Bangladesh.

The event provided a platform for knowledge sharing, industry engagement and strategic discussions on the evolving role of artificial intelligence (AI), hyper-converged infrastructure (HCI), and innovative enterprise technology solutions in supporting modern business needs.

The programme commenced with Shehan Rajudin, group business manager – South Asia at Inflow Technologies, who delivered an overview of Inflow Technologies, its business operations and its role in bringing technology solutions to the regional market.

Leo Tao, Sales Vice President – SEA Region at xFusion International, introduced xFusion and presented an overview of the company’s business and technology capabilities. Following this, Md Omur Faruk, Deputy Sales Director, xFusion International Co Ltd, SEA Region, provided an overview of xFusion’s comprehensive product portfolio, highlighting its range of enterprise technology solutions.

A key highlight of the event was the presentation on xFusion TokenBox, delivered by Chen Honglun (Allen), Sales Director at xFusion International. The session explored the solution in detail and provided attendees with insights into its capabilities and potential applications.

The technical segment featured Pronab Sarker, Senior Technical Consultant at Inflow Technologies, who delivered a presentation on the FusionOne HCI Solution. His session focused on the solution’s technical capabilities and its relevance to enterprise IT infrastructure requirements.

The event also featured a panel discussion titled “xFusion Tech Day – Bangladesh,” bringing together senior technology and business leaders to exchange perspectives on enterprise technology, infrastructure modernisation and the evolving digital landscape. The panel comprised: Vandia Yang, GM & President – SEA, xFusion, Leo Tao, Sales Vice President – SEA, xFusion, Md Faisal Hossain, EVP & Group CTO, BD Finance, Md Mahbubul Alam (Rafel), CISO, Prime Bank Ltd.

The discussion offered an opportunity to examine the challenges and opportunities facing enterprises as they modernize their IT environments, strengthen their technology capabilities and prepare for an increasingly AI-driven business landscape.

Through product presentations, technical insights and interactive discussions, xFusion Tech Day – Bangladesh reinforced the importance of collaboration among technology providers, distribution partners and enterprise customers in advancing innovation and enabling digital transformation.

The event concluded with a shared emphasis on strengthening partnerships, exchanging industry knowledge and exploring technology-driven opportunities to support the future growth of Bangladesh’s enterprise technology ecosystem.

item.title: Garment workers try to take to the streets through Mirpur alleys, police disperse them
item.description:
Garment factory workers are making scattered attempts to take to the streets through various alleys in Mirpur, in the capital.

At around 10:45 am today, Monday, workers tried to come out onto the main road through an alley in the Senpara Parbata area of Mirpur-10. Police chased them to disperse the group and fired several tear gas shells.

Later, workers also tried to take to the streets in the Proshika intersection area beside the stadium in Mirpur-2. Police drove them away.

Eyewitnesses said workers were arriving in small, scattered groups from the Rupnagar area, passing by the stadium in Mirpur-2 towards Proshika intersection. They tried to come out onto the road.

Police obstructed them at around 11:00 am, triggering a tense situation between the police and the workers.

Dhaka-Tangail highway blocked again by garment workers, BGB deployed

Earlier, at around 10:45 am, workers had tried to come out onto the road through an alley in the Senpara Parbata area of Mirpur-10. Police fired several tear gas shells to disperse them. The workers later moved away from the area.

Following two consecutive days of protests and clashes involving garment workers in Mirpur, members of the police and other law enforcement agencies have been on alert since Monday morning.

Police personnel were seen deployed around the Mirpur-10 roundabout and in nearby areas from early morning. Riot-control vehicles, water cannons and other vehicles were kept ready at the roundabout.

Traffic on the roads in and around Mirpur-10 is moving normally. There have been no disruptions, and pedestrians and general public are moving about without hindrance. The situation in the area appeared normal at around 10:30 am.

PM holds meeting over garment workers’ violent protests

Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) Joint Commissioner (Crime Prevention–North) Mohidul Islam briefed journalists on Monday morning on the situation surrounding the workers’ movement in Mirpur and the police presence on alert.

Mohidul Islam said police were investigating whether anyone was seeking to create disorder, disrupt public safety or conspire to damage state property in connection with the workers’ movement in Mirpur.

An investigation was under way to identify those involved in Sunday’s clashes and the attack on a police vehicle. Police activities, including the collection of intelligence, were continuing, said the police official.

Mohidul Islam said workers were not the only people involved in Sunday’s incident; the investigation had also found the involvement of other criminals alongside the workers. Legal action would be taken against them. Anyone causing harm to the country by violating the law would face strict legal action, he said.

Government forms new wage board to increase garment workers’ salaries

When asked how many people had been arrested in Sunday’s incident, Mohidul Islam said around 25 people had been arrested from different locations. No one had been arrested so far today. However, those who had tried to gather at various locations have been dispersed, he said.

On the police presence, Mohidul Islam said members of the force had been deployed at various locations and their operations were continuing. They remained on high alert, and necessary measures were being taken to keep the situation normal.

On Sunday, garment factory workers blocked the road at the Mirpur-10 intersection in the capital, demanding that the monthly minimum wage be raised to Tk 30,000. Workers from several garment factories took to the streets at around 8:00 am, disrupting traffic in nearby areas.

3 metro stations in Mirpur closed for hours amid garment workers’ protests

Clashes between workers and police began at around 11:15 am. According to eyewitnesses, police used batons, water cannons, sound grenades and tear gas shells to disperse the workers. The workers then threw bricks and stones at police from various directions.

Clashes and chases between the two sides continued until around 11:45 am. At one point around midday, a police vehicle was set on fire beneath Mirpur-11 metro station. Due to the clashes, Mirpur-10, Mirpur-11 and Pallabi metro stations remained closed from 11:38 am to 1:58 pm.

The previous day, Saturday, garment workers had also blocked roads in Mirpur over the same demand. From 10:30 am to 1:00 pm, traffic came to a standstill in and around Mirpur-10, Mirpur-11 and Mirpur-12.

item.title: Sheikh Abdul Hye flees to Canada after ‘plundering’ BASIC Bank
item.description:
“I am the scapegoat”—that was how former BASIC Bank chairman Sheikh Abdul Hye, also known as Bacchu, described himself.

Although he claims to be innocent, Abdul Hye has been accused of turning one of the best state-owned banks into one of the worst. He has also been accused of embezzling huge sums of money.

Abdul Hye has been in hiding over these allegations. He had been out of sight for several years. Eventually, I managed to obtain his mobile phone number. I spoke to him several times in July, August and September. His voice was familiar, and I had no difficulty recognising him.

Abdul Hye responded to the allegations against him and tried to deny them. However, several investigations by Bangladesh Bank have substantiated the allegations, leaving little room for him to evade responsibility.

At one point, he said he was not the only one who had approved irregular loans at BASIC Bank; leaders of the then Awami League government were also responsible. He added, “Don’t make me the fall guy.”

Before hearing the full story from Abdul Hye, we need to turn back the pages of history by three decades. Bangladesh Small Industries and Commerce Bank PLC, commonly known as BASIC Bank, was established in 1989.

The bank was once a trusted institution for small and medium-sized entrepreneurs. By convention, the secretary of the Ministry of Industries served as its chairman. From its establishment until Abdul Hye took over as chairman, the bank’s default loan ratio had never exceeded 3–4 per cent. Until 2008, it was recognised as one of the country’s best banks.

The Awami League came to power after winning the parliamentary election held in December 2008 under the military-backed caretaker government. It took office in January 2009. On 10 September that year, Sheikh Abdul Hye was appointed chairman of the BASIC Bank board.

Abdul Hye remained chairman for two consecutive terms, until July 2014. During those nearly five years, loan irregularities and corruption involving Tk 45 billion took place at the bank. The government later injected Tk 35 billion from the state exchequer to bail it out. That money came from taxpayers. Yet the bank collapsed and never managed to recover.

There is a complex, multifaceted story behind how one of the biggest scandals in the country’s banking sector unfolded. Statements from several former BASIC Bank directors and other relevant people indicate that then Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina appointed and protected Abdul Hye. At the same time, officials of the then Directorate General of Forces Intelligence (DGFI) exerted pressure to prevent media reports about his corruption.

Prothom Alo, however, continued publishing reports on the scandal. Abdul Hye is now accused in at least 66 cases filed by the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC). But where is he now?

The ACC says he is still in Bangladesh. Our investigation, however, has found that he is in Canada with his family. The Awami League government fell on 5 August 2024 following the July mass uprising. Abdul Hye had left the country a year earlier, in 2023. He did not say which month he left.

Arrest warrant issued against Basic Bank's Bachhu, family members
How BASIC Bank’s Abdul Hye Bacchu bade adieu with ‘dignity’

How he became BASIC Bank chairman

In several rounds of phone conversations lasting hours, conducted across the Atlantic Ocean, Abdul Hye recounted in his own way how he became chairman of BASIC Bank.

He was a Jatiya Party leader. He was elected a member of parliament from Bagerhat-1 in the 1986 election and later served as chairman of the district council. After the fall of the Ershad government in 1990, he became inactive in national politics.

As BASIC Bank was state-owned, the secretary of the Ministry of Industries would generally serve as its chairman. The Awami League government broke with this established practice by appointing Abdul Hye to the post.

Abdul Hye told Prothom Alo that during the military-backed caretaker government in 2007–08, he lived in a flat in Dhaka’s Banani area. The then army chief, Moeen U Ahmed, was president of the flat owners’ association by virtue of his position. Abdul Hye was its joint general secretary.

He said, “At that time, I was in regular contact with the army chief. We communicated about various matters. I used that connection to my advantage at the time. I don’t want to say what I used it for.”

Former army chief Moeen U Ahmed has been living abroad for many years. Prothom Alo contacted him by phone and sent him questions seeking his response to Abdul Hye’s claims, but received no reply.

Meanwhile, Abdul Hye said, “I had no connection with the Awami League, and I still don’t. Sheikh Hasina could not stand me because I was from the Jatiya Party.”

When Abdul Hye was appointed chairman of BASIC Bank, Abul Maal Abdul Muhith (now deceased) was finance minister.

Muhith had expressed his frustration with Abdul Hye on several occasions, but he was powerless. He once described Abdul Hye’s activities at BASIC Bank as “almost like robbery”. In parliament, he even said that members of his own party were obstructing efforts to catch the fraudsters (30 June 2016).

Abul Maal Abdul Muhith died on 30 April 2022. Former army chief Moeen U Ahmed is abroad. As a result, it has not been possible to establish clearly why the Awami League appointed Abdul Hye as BASIC Bank chairman. What is clear, however, is that Abdul Hye had influence over the Awami League government. It was that government that enabled him to cross the Atlantic instead of going to prison.

BASIC Bank sunk in broad daylight  
BASIC, National Bank evade merger for now

A former BASIC Bank director, speaking to Prothom Alo on condition of anonymity, said, “At one point, then Finance Minister Abul Maal Abdul Muhith called me to find out what was happening at BASIC Bank. After hearing everything, he told me that Abdul Hye Bacchu needed to be removed. But in the end, even he could not do it.”

Alongside appointing Abdul Hye, the Awami League government reconstituted the boards of four state-owned banks—Sonali, Janata, Agrani and BASIC—in September 2010. Appointments were made on political considerations. A Prothom Alo report published on its front page on 11 September 2010 carried the headline: “Boards of four banks reconstituted by rewarding party leaders and supporters.”

BASIC Bank scam: Where’s Abdul Hye

‘Corruption began’ with the purchase of a building

Three months after Abdul Hye became chairman, a meeting of the BASIC Bank board was held on 13 December 2009. According to bank documents, Abdul Hye proposed at the meeting that BASIC Bank build its own headquarters. Four months later, on 1 April 2010, the bank signed an agreement worth Tk 810 million to purchase a building under construction in Motijheel.

But the agreement was unregistered. Such agreements are not admissible in court. It stated that the building would be named “Zaman-BASIC Bank Tower”. The land was owned by Sinku Akramuzzaman. A construction company owned by him was named Business Resources Limited. Under the agreement, Business Resources was to construct the building. In other words, both the sale of the land and the construction of the building were controlled by the same person.

A Bangladesh Bank investigation in 2012 found that Tk 400 million had been released from the bank on the very day the agreement was signed. Before construction had even begun, arrangements were hurriedly made to pay the amount through Niranjan Debnath, then deputy general manager of BASIC Bank and now managing director of the Investment Corporation of Bangladesh (ICB). He was promoted to general manager shortly afterwards.

Niranjan Debnath told Prothom Alo last Saturday that a subcommittee had been formed to implement the board’s decision on the building. The committee recommended that Tk 400 million be paid urgently. He said the situation had become so bad that no one, including the managing director, could speak up because the chairman had everyone at gunpoint.

Another Tk 360 million was paid in several instalments over the following two years as the price of the building, bringing the total payment to Tk 760 million.

But ownership of the land remained disputed. It was listed as abandoned property, and a legal case was pending. The bank has still not gained full possession of the building.

Asked why he had signed an unregistered agreement, Abdul Hye told Prothom Alo, “The lawyer at the time would be in a better position to explain that. I don’t remember the details.”

The bank’s current management, however, says that a review of the documents shows Abdul Hye played the leading role in the decision to proceed despite the disputed land ownership, the unregistered agreement and the large payments. It also alleges that he personally benefited from the deal, while the bank suffered losses.

BASIC Bank’s current chairman, Helal Ahmed Chowdhury, told Prothom Alo, “We are waiting to move into the building. It will save us the cost of rent.”

BASIC Bank scam: Court orders to seize assets of Abdul Hye

Loans disbursed at will

During Abdul Hye’s tenure as BASIC Bank chairman, the bank’s lending increased at an extraordinary rate. According to Bangladesh Bank data, the bank’s loans stood at around Tk 46.34 billion in 2010. By 2012, the amount had nearly doubled, but profits had declined.

BASIC Bank’s profits in 2010 and 2011 were around Tk 660 million and Tk 970 million, respectively. In 2012, profits fell to around Tk 30 million.

The bank made a loss in 2013 and never returned to profitability. In an interview with Prothom Alo on 12 January 2020, the late Finance Minister Abul Maal Abdul Muhith said, “A man like Abdul Hye Bacchu single-handedly destroyed BASIC Bank.”

When Abdul Hye Bacchu was appointed chairman, A K M Sajedur Rahman was BASIC Bank’s managing director. He served at the bank from 23 July 2008 to 27 December 2010.

On 27 October, Sajedur Rahman spoke to Prothom Alo for about an hour at the office of an organisation in Dhaka, recalling the events of that period. He said, “Within a few months of Sheikh Abdul Hye joining the bank, I realised what kind of person he was. He did not follow the bank’s rules and regulations. Even when I saw all this, I had no way of leaving the bank because he constantly threatened me, saying I could not leave.”

Sajedur Rahman said, “One day, I secretly sought the help of the then governor, Atiur Rahman. I told him everything and said that no banking was taking place there; rather, there was an attempt to stripping depositors’ money.”

He said, “Even after hearing everything, Atiur Rahman gave me no assurance of support. He told me about his own helplessness. When I returned, Sheikh Abdul Hye asked me with a faint smile, ‘Did you go to see the governor?’ I thought someone at Bangladesh Bank must have informed Bacchu that I had met the governor. I did not deny it either.”

Sajedur Rahman went to Australia for medical treatment towards the end of 2010. His leave began on 2 November that year, and he returned on 25 December. He said that after returning, he was asked to rejoin the bank, but he did not. On 27 December, he submitted his resignation through an intermediary.

To illustrate the nature of Abdul Hye’s relationship with then Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, Sajedur Rahman recalled an incident. He said that after the fire at Nimtali in Old Dhaka on 3 June 2010, the bank’s board decided to donate Tk 5 million to the then prime minister’s relief fund.

“The bank chairman took me with him to Ganabhaban to hand over the donation cheque to Sheikh Hasina. As soon as she saw him from a distance, she said, ‘What is it, Bacchu? Why are you here?’ Abdul Hye Bacchu replied, ‘Apa, I have come to make a donation following the Nimtali fire.’ Sheikh Hasina said, ‘That’s good, very good.’”

Sajedur Rahman said Abdul Hye’s relationship with Sheikh Hasina was so close that she addressed him informally as “tui”.

After Sajedur Rahman resigned, Kazi Fakhrul Islam became BASIC Bank’s managing director. An ACC source said he fled to Malaysia after being removed from his post on 26 May 2014.

One irregularity after another

A review of Prothom Alo’s archive shows that, following allegations of irregularities, Bangladesh Bank began special inspections at various BASIC Bank branches towards the end of 2012. Irregularities were found at several branches, including Gulshan, Dilkusha and Shantinagar.

The findings revealed that around Tk 45 billion had been siphoned off from the bank in the name of loans between 2009 and 2013. Most of the loans had been disbursed without proper scrutiny.

In September 2012, then Bangladesh Bank Governor Atiur Rahman warned BASIC Bank’s managing director Kazi Fakhrul Islam and other senior officials. The central bank sent a letter to the Financial Institutions Division. Later, on 17 July 2013, Bangladesh Bank and BASIC Bank signed a memorandum of understanding. But the loan irregularities continued.

On 18 August 2013, then Finance Minister Abul Maal Abdul Muhith held a meeting with the chairmen and managing directors of state-owned banks. Abdul Hye was asked to attend but did not show up.

Bangladesh Bank subsequently sent a more strongly worded letter to the Financial Institutions Division, saying that lending discipline at the bank had collapsed.

In May 2014, Bangladesh Bank recommended that the government dissolve BASIC Bank’s board and removed managing director Kazi Fakhrul Islam that same month. Two months later, in July 2014, Sheikh Abdul Hye stepped down as chairman. On 4 July, he went to the residence of then Finance Minister Abul Maal Abdul Muhith and submitted his resignation. The following day, 5 July, was the scheduled end of his term.

Speaking from Canada about the bank’s irregularities, Abdul Hye said, “Was I the only one who approved every proposal? The entire process of implementing the decisions involved other board members and officials. The fact that the chairman’s signature is on a document does not mean he can be made solely responsible for the entire process.”

Abdul Hye also alleged that Sheikh Helal Uddin, a cousin of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, had unlawfully interfered in the bank’s affairs. He claimed that Nilufar Ahmed, then director general at the Prime Minister’s Office and a close associate of Sheikh Hasina, wielded enormous influence over the bank. Anwarul Islam, then presidium member of the Jubo League, and the bank’s then managing director Kazi Fakhrul Islam were also influential, he said.

It has not been possible to establish where Nilufar Ahmed and Anwarul Islam are now.

Speaking from Canada, Abdul Hye said he was being made a “scapegoat” because he was being blamed as chairman without investigating the entire loan process and identifying all those responsible.

However, letters written by two directors at the time point to Abdul Hye’s responsibility. On 11 July 2013, A K M Rezaur Rahman, a board member and former additional secretary, wrote to M Aslam Alam, then secretary of the Financial Institutions Division. A few days earlier, he had also met the secretary with another director, accountant A K M Kamrul Islam.

The letter referred to a board meeting held on 30 April 2013. Rezaur Rahman wrote that when Bangladesh Bank’s questions about 13 irregular loans came up, Abdul Hye had said, “There is no need to discuss this.” When the chairman tried to move on to the next agenda item, Rezaur Rahman objected. He wrote that he had said the board could not proceed without discussing such a letter from Bangladesh Bank.

Rezaur Rahman also wrote that, often, documents relating to loans and investments worth hundreds of crores of taka were distributed on the night before board meetings, leaving directors no time to read them. Photographs of the chairman with Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina were displayed at the bank’s head office and lobby. The chairman would often tell the board, “Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina is my elder sister. I don’t care about anyone except her.”

In his letter, Rezaur Rahman said that reports on BASIC Bank’s irregularities were being published in newspapers one after another, and the issue had also been discussed in parliament. Given the situation, he said, he felt like stepping down from the board, but his conscience told him that he should at least continue to act as a watchdog in the bank’s interest.

The two dissenting directors, Rezaur Rahman and Kamrul Islam, were later unable to remain on BASIC Bank’s board. The government subsequently appointed the former to Sonali Bank and the latter to Janata Bank as directors.

A Bangladesh Bank official involved in supervising BASIC Bank told Prothom Alo that armed personnel from government agencies would also attend board meetings. As a result, whatever the chairman said would be approved. In such circumstances, no one had any opportunity to do anything.

Dissenting director Rezaur Rahman died several years ago at a hospital in Thailand. When contacted, Kamrul Islam asked me to visit his chartered accountancy firm in Mirpur, Dhaka. I went there on 5 July and spoke with him at length.

Recalling the events during his time as a BASIC Bank director, Kamrul Islam sighed. He said, “The letter gives a full account of how the bank was ruined under Abdul Hye’s leadership. I think it is rare anywhere in the world for a good bank to be brought to the brink of destruction over such a long period, despite the existence of a government and so many state agencies.”

Officials serving in several important government institutions were on BASIC Bank’s board. Directors received an allowance of Tk 8,000 for each board meeting. Yet, while the bank was sinking, the careers of several board members advanced rapidly.

Alongside Abdul Hye, two then directors general of the Prime Minister’s Office, Shubh Asish Basu and Nilufar Ahmed, were appointed to BASIC Bank’s board. Shubh Asish Basu later became commerce secretary. On 28 January 2024, Nilufar Ahmed was appointed special assistant to Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina with the rank of secretary. Both are now accused in cases.

Another person appointed as a BASIC Bank director alongside Abdul Hye was Bijoy Bhattacharya, then joint secretary at the Ministry of Finance. He later became vice-chairman of the Export Promotion Bureau (EPB).

Kamrunnahar Ahmed served as a BASIC Bank director throughout the scandal. She later became additional secretary of the Financial Institutions Division. Bijoy Bhattacharya and Kamrunnahar Ahmed are now retired. They, too, are accused.

Other members of the board alongside Abdul Hye included former chairman of the Bangladesh Economic Zones Authority (now abolished) Fakhrul Islam and former secretary of the Information and Communication Technology Division Shyam Sundar Sikder.

After retirement, Shyam Sundar Sikder was also appointed chairman of the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC). Both are now accused.

Among the directors from the private sector were Jahangir Akhand Salim, then president of the Chandpur Chamber of Commerce; former customs commissioner Shakhawat Hossain; Kazi Akhtar Hossain, then chairman of the Department of Accounting and Information Systems at Islamic University, Kushtia; and Anwarul Islam, managing director of a company named ARS Louvre Bangladesh.

Kazi Akhtar Hossain told Prothom Alo on 5 July that Sheikh Abdul Hye wielded such power that no director, including himself, could play a proper role on the board. Asked why he had not resigned, he replied, “That could have been done.”

Abdul Hye’s Sudden Wealth

In 2013, Bangladesh Bank investigated the link between the BASIC Bank scandal and the increase in Abdul Hye’s personal wealth. His assets included 30 kathas of land in the cantonment area, an apartment, 138 kathas of land in Bashundhara, and eight deep-sea fishing trawlers purchased for hundreds of crores of taka.

The assets were held in the names of Abdul Hye, his wife Sheikh Shirin Akhtar, son Sheikh Sabid Hye Anik, daughter Sheikh Rafa Hye, and brother Sheikh Shahriar, also known as Panna.

The trawlers were purchased within a year of his appointment as chairman. Six were registered in the name of Eden Fisheries and two in the name of Crown Fisheries. Their market value was around Tk 1 billion. The Bangladesh Financial Intelligence Unit (BFIU) investigated the matter in 2014 and sent a report to the ACC.

The investigation found that nearly Tk 200 million had been transferred to two bank accounts belonging to Sheikh Shahriar from several companies that had received loans from BASIC Bank.

The trawlers were purchased from former Jatiya Party lawmaker Mahjabin Morshed and her husband, Morshed Murad Ibrahim, former president of the Chattogram Chamber of Commerce. At the time, they had loans worth Tk 450 crore from BASIC Bank.

Meanwhile, more than 30 kathas of land were purchased inside the cantonment area. In August 2012, Sheikh Abdul Hye signed an agreement to purchase the land for Tk 1.1 billion with Amin Ahmed, chairman of Best Holdings Group.

The land was purchased in the names of five people, including Abdul Hye, his wife, son, daughter and brother. The total deed value of the property was shown as Tk 152.5 million. Some of the pay orders used to pay for the land came from BASIC Bank customers.

One of the companies that issued the pay orders was Jamuna Agro Chemicals. Its co-owner and former Jatiya Party lawmaker Shawkat Chowdhury told Prothom Alo in 2020 that he had to bribe Abdul Hye because securing a loan was not easy.

In 2012, Sheikh Abdul Hye also purchased 138 kathas of land in Block I of Bashundhara Residential Area. At market prices, the land was worth nearly Tk 3 billion.

Speaking from Canada, Abdul Hye now says he paid for the cantonment land gradually and that all his assets were purchased with legitimate money. He said, “There is proof that I sold my house in Dhanmondi. I was not poor. I had a business in the real estate sector.”

However, officials at Bangladesh Bank and the ACC say both agencies have evidence that Sheikh Abdul Hye and his brother received commissions as bribes in exchange for loans.

66 Cases

Allegations of bribery, irregularities and corruption against the board led by Sheikh Abdul Hye had emerged while he was still chairman. After his term ended, the ACC filed 56 cases in September 2015, followed by three more. However, neither Abdul Hye nor any board member was named as an accused in any of those cases.

From 2011 to 2016, former President Mohammed Shahabuddin served as an ACC commissioner. There is speculation that Abdul Hye received protection from the ACC during that period. Later, following a court order, the ACC was compelled to summon Sheikh Abdul Hye and other board members. But they were not named as accused in the cases.

Iqbal Mahmood served as ACC chairman for five consecutive years, from 2016 to 2021. It was not possible to contact him. An explanation for his silence on Sheikh Abdul Hye, however, can be found in an earlier statement. In an interview with Prothom Alo on 12 April 2018, Iqbal Mahmood said, “There is no scope to accuse someone based on emotion or assumptions. I will not be able to prove in court that he took bribes.”

Finally, amid criticism, the ACC completed the charge sheets in 59 cases related to the embezzlement of BASIC Bank funds on 12 June 2023. Abdul Hye was named as an accused in 58 of them.

At the time, Moinuddin Abdullah was ACC chairman. After his name appeared in the charge sheets, an arrest warrant was issued against Abdul Hye. But he was never arrested and did not surrender to the court. He had left the country before his name appeared in the charge sheets.

On 9 February 2025, during the interim government’s tenure, the ACC filed three cases simultaneously against Abdul Hye and his family. The first was against Abdul Hye. The allegation is that, through forgery and fraud, he embezzled loan funds and accumulated assets worth Tk 1.25 billion beyond his known sources of income. Of this amount, he allegedly laundered nearly Tk 560 million to Canada.

The second case was filed against his wife, Sheikh Shirin Akhtar. She is accused of owning assets worth Tk 370 million beyond her known sources of income. Sheikh Abdul Hye is also an accused in this case. The third case was filed against his son, Sheikh Sabid Hye Anik. The ACC alleges that he owns assets worth Tk 450 million beyond his known sources of income. Sheikh Abdul Hye is a co-accused in this case as well.

In March 2025, three more cases were filed against Abdul Hye and his family members. Another case was filed later. The ACC says the total number of cases now stands at 66.

On the allegations of money laundering, Sheikh Abdul Hye says the evidence should be made public. He argues that it is wrong to hold him responsible without proof. According to him, various steps were taken against him in 2023 to gain political advantage in the 2024 election.

But it is evident that the Awami League government allowed Abdul Hye to leave the country without obstruction. Three weeks after the BNP government came to power, on 9 March, a court imposed a travel ban on Abdul Hye and 15 others, including board members, managing directors and deputy managing directors who served during his tenure.

ACC Commissioner (Investigation) Md Sajjad Hossain Bhuiyan told Prothom Alo last Saturday that charge sheets had been submitted in 60 of the 66 cases related to the BASIC Bank scandal. However, the court returned all the charge sheets with certain observations. The charge sheets in the remaining six cases are also being prepared. He said, “We will make the necessary corrections and submit all the charge sheets to the court very soon.”

Asked why the court had returned the charge sheets, Sazzad Hossain Bhuiyan said, “The accused were selected arbitrarily in these cases. Among those who served on the bank’s board at the same time, some were named as accused while others were left out. It was a pick-and-choose approach.”

Others Who Also Failed

There are many examples of irregularities at BASIC Bank. For instance, during Abdul Hye’s tenure as chairman, the bank’s Gulshan branch lent Tk 790 million to Asian Food Trading. As soon as it received the loan, the company deposited part of the money into Abdul Hye’s bank account and another portion into the account of his brother, Sheikh Shahriar. Bangladesh Bank later found that the two brothers had received Tk 300 million in this way from a single customer.

Irregularities were not limited to lending; recruitment was also manipulated. Between 2012 and 2014, BASIC Bank recruited 1,173 people without following any of the rules regarding educational qualifications, age limits, written and oral examinations or recruitment procedures. A 2014 report by the Office of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) described the recruitment as “unprecedented”.

A Bangladesh Bank investigation found that the bank’s IT department opened the door to loans without written approval from the head office, while branch offices created loans at will. The treasury department continuously supplied funds to the branches. Yet no one from these departments faced punishment.

The bank’s human resources department was controlled by then managing director Kazi Fakhrul Islam and two deputy managing directors, A Monayem Khan and Ruhul Alam. The other two deputy managing directors, Fazlus Sobahan and Anup Kumar Purokayastha, controlled all the branches in Chattogram.

According to BASIC Bank sources, Ruhul Alam was a retired army officer. Despite having no banking experience, Abdul Hye directly appointed him as deputy general manager (DGM) in April 2012. Seven months later, before his employment had even been made permanent, he was promoted to general manager (GM). Within a year, he was made a deputy managing director (DMD).

The board documents cited “exceptionally excellent performance” as the reason for his promotion. Yet the rules required at least three years of experience as a DGM and at least 18 years of banking experience to be promoted to GM.

After the end of Sheikh Abdul Hye’s tenure, the bank’s former managing director Alauddin A Majid became chairman. Loans disbursed during his tenure have also since become classified as defaulted. Asked about this, Alauddin A Majid told Prothom Alo, “We tried to improve the bank. It had fallen so deep into trouble that we could not fully turn it around.”

Taxpayers’ Money to Keep the Bank Afloat

In April 2024, an attempt was made to merge the struggling BASIC Bank with City Bank, but the plan did not proceed. According to BASIC Bank data, as of the end of last September, the bank’s loans stood at Tk 107.6 billion, of which 60 per cent, or Tk 64.14 billion, was classified as defaulted. The bank has recently asked the government for Tk 50 billion.

The bank’s current chairman, Helal Ahmed Chowdhury, told Prothom Alo, “Let the past be dealt with according to the law. We have asked the government for a Tk 50 billion deposit at a low interest rate to improve the bank. If we receive it, the bank will be able to recover. Deposits have increased over the past year, and defaulted loans have declined.”

The BNP government now has to inject taxpayers’ money to keep afloat banks that were looted during the Awami League’s tenure. At an event on 11 October, Bangladesh Bank Governor Mostaqur Rahman said that, to overcome the damage inflicted on the banking sector by looting during the Awami League era, Tk 600 billion would be needed annually from the national budget over the next five to eight years. Bangladesh Bank has submitted a draft proposal on the matter to the government.

Mostaqur Rahman said, “The money that was embezzled belonged to the people. Now those same people will have to pay it back.”

Whatever Abdul Hye may say, he must take responsibility for the BASIC Bank scandal, said Muinul Islam, a retired professor of economics at the University of Chittagong. He told Prothom Alo that unless those responsible for bringing the bank to this state are given exemplary punishment, it will send the wrong message to the banking sector.

item.title: Nine dead in small plane crash near Trump's Florida home
item.description:
US-PLANE-CRASHES-NEAR-PALM-BEACH,-FLORIDA

A Learjet plummeted into a neighborhood in southern Florida miles from US President Donald Trump's resort home on Sunday, killing all nine people on board, officials said.

Several unverified clips posted to social media depicting the deadly crash showed an aircraft nearly vertical slamming at high speed into the ground, creating a large fireball and leaving a flaming crater near a busy roadside.

"Today's plane crash in Palm Beach County, Florida is a horrific tragedy," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement, confirming that all nine people on the aircraft were killed.

Duffy said the plane, a Learjet 60, had departed from Austin, Texas and was headed for the Bahamas.

The crash occurred near Cresthaven, a neighborhood in Palm Beach County that is less than seven miles (11 kilometers) from Trump''s resort home Mar-a-Lago.

"Obviously this is a cataclysmic plane crash," Florida Governor Ron DeSantis told reporters near the scene.

"It looked like a missile going down," he said, adding there were no reports of anyone on the ground being injured.

Trump had been at Mar-a-Lago on Sunday but departed from the nearby and newly renamed President Donald J. Trump International Airport shortly after he boarded Air Force One at 11:55 am (1655 GMT), about an hour before the crash of the Learjet aircraft.

The plane came down near the entrance to a mobile home park, Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores said, noting about 600 residents were evacuated and relocated to shelters.

"The FAA and National Transportation Safety Board will investigate" the crash, the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement.
Storms had been reported in the area. Trump carried an umbrella as he boarded Air Force One.

In an audio recording posted to air traffic website liveatc.net, someone in the cockpit can be heard reporting "moderate turbulence" and saying the crew was "managing the ice."

The person said the plane was "picking up precipitation" and needed "to climb" shortly before saying: "Mayday, mayday, we''re descending 10,000 feet per minute."

Seconds later, the person said they were "declaring an emergency" as the plane descended 20,000 feet per minute.

"We''re going to crash into the ground," the person said, shortly before communications stopped.

item.title: Filipino woman injured in Banani gas explosion dies
item.description:
A Filipino woman who suffered burns in a fire caused by a gas stove leak at a Banani house, Dhaka, has died.

Kristine Ver Bunag (32) died at around 3:20am on Monday while undergoing treatment in the intensive care unit (ICU) of the National Institute of Burn and Plastic Surgery.

Sultan Mahmud Sikder, resident physician at the institute, said 63 per cent of her body had been burnt.

Kristine suffered the burns last Wednesday (28 October) morning when a fire broke out due to a gas leak as she tried to light the stove for cooking at a house on Road 7 in Banani.

She was rescued and taken to a local hospital before being transferred to the National Institute of Burn and Plastic Surgery.

Al-Amin, the building manager of the apartment in Banani, said Kristine had arrived in Bangladesh on 15 October on a tourist visa.

She had rented the house for two months with a Japanese national.

Al-Amin added that Kristine was burnt while trying to light the stove to cook in the morning. The Japanese national was not at home at the time of the incident.

item.title: 1 detained over ‘Facebook post’ about setting fire to police vehicle in Mirpur
item.description:
Police have detained a man over allegations that he set fire to a police vehicle in Mirpur area of the capital. Police said the man had posted on his Facebook account claiming that he had set fire to the police vehicle.

Police detained the man, identified as Rajib Chandra Das, from the Mirpur area early on Monday. In addition, police detained 20 more people during raids in different parts of Dhaka on Sunday night over allegations of setting fire to and vandalising police vehicles.

Sabotage plot under guise of labour protest in Mirpur, 29 detained

Pallabi Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Jalal Uddin told Prothom Alo, “Rajib was detained early this morning. We have not questioned him yet.”

On Sunday, garment workers blocked roads and staged demonstrations in Mirpur, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk 30,000.

Clashes and chases between the workers and police took place repeatedly from the morning until 1:00 pm. At one point, protesters set fire to a police vehicle beneath the Mirpur-11 Metro Rail Station.

Garment workers clash with police at Mirpur-10

Police said they had detained 19 people from different parts of Mirpur on Sunday afternoon over their alleged involvement in the incident.

Additional Deputy Commissioner (ADC) of the Mirpur Division of Police Zahidul Islam told Prothom Alo, “We conducted raids in different parts of Dhaka last night and detained many more people over allegations of setting fire to police vehicles. The operation is still underway. We will be able to confirm the actual number once it is over.”

item.title: Dhaka-Tangail highway blocked again by garment workers, BGB deployed
item.description:
Garment workers have once again staged a protest on the Dhaka-Tangail highway in Kaliakair upazila of Gazipur, demanding that the minimum monthly wage be raised to Tk 30,000.

They blocked the highway in the Chandra Palli Bidyut area from 7:00am on Monday.

The blockade has caused traffic congestion stretching at least 10km on both sides of the highway, leaving passengers and drivers travelling to different destinations in distress.

According to police and local sources, a group of workers gathered in the Chandra Palli Bidyut area on Monday morning and took to the highway to stage a demonstration. More people later joined them, bringing traffic to a halt on both sides.

Kaliakair Police Station Officer-in-Charge Shahidul Islam said efforts were under way to resolve the situation through talks with the workers.

He claimed that a group of workers and outsiders had gathered in the Chandra Palli Bidyut area and blocked the highway before launching a demonstration demanding higher wages.

Gazipur Deputy Commissioner Md Nurul Karim Bhuiyan said 10 platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) personnel had been deployed from Monday to control the workers’ movement. Executive magistrates would also be on duty alongside them, he added.

Earlier, garment workers began protesting and blocking roads from Sunday morning in Chandra Palli Bidyut, Safipur Bazar, Mouchak and Telichala in Kaliakair.

PM holds meeting over garment workers’ violent protests
3 metro stations in Mirpur closed for hours amid garment workers’ protests

Amid tensions throughout the day, a fabric scrap (jhut) warehouse of a garment factory and a police van were set on fire in the Chandra Palli Bidyut area around 12:30pm. The incidents spread panic in the area. Law enforcement personnel later stepped in to bring the situation under control.

At least 30 factories declared holidays amid the daylong protests, road blockades and violence. Traffic on the highway returned to normal after about six hours.

Police said allegations had also emerged that outsiders had joined the workers’ movement and instigated unrest.

In pictures: Police use tear gas, water cannons as garment workers clash in Mirpur
Garment workers’ protests: At least 80 factories shut in Gazipur and Savar

On Sunday, police arrested nine members of Chhatra League, Swechchhasebak League and Sramik League in raids across different parts of Kaliakair. Police claimed they were arrested on charges of directly participating in and instigating the workers' protests.

Gazipur district and metropolitan police have also arrested a total of 30 people, police said.

Home minister holds meeting with garment owners to resolve workers' unrest
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed on Monday held a meeting at the Secretariat with leaders of garment factory owners as part of the government's efforts to resolve the ongoing unrest in the readymade garment (RMG) sector and restore normalcy in industrial areas.
The meeting was convened following Sunday's violent demonstrations by garment workers in Dhaka, Gazipur, Savar, Ashulia and Tangail, where protesters demanded a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000.
The government has taken initiatives to address the situation through dialogue with industry stakeholders while maintaining law and order and ensuring the uninterrupted operation of the country's vital export-oriented garment sector.
During Sunday's demonstrations, several areas witnessed clashes between protesters and law enforcement personnel, road blockades and incidents of vandalism targeting factories and vehicles.
Meanwhile, police arrested 19 leaders and activists of the Awami League and its affiliated organisations, including the banned Bangladesh Chhatra League and Jubo League, in Dhaka on allegations of instigating the demonstrations.
The government has also formed a six-member minimum wage board to review the existing salary structure of garment workers, with representation from workers, employers, the government and an independent member.
At present, the minimum monthly wage for garment workers stands at Tk12,500. Workers are demanding Tk30,000, citing rising living costs, including house rent, food, transportation and healthcare expenses.
The government has called upon workers to return to their workplaces and pursue their demands through dialogue and peaceful negotiations, rather than resorting to violence, vandalism and road blockades.
The BGMEA has expressed concern that prolonged unrest could disrupt production, delay export shipments and affect Bangladesh's commitments to international buyers.

item.title: Police disperse garment workers after fresh clashes in Mirpur
item.description:
Clashes broke out between garment workers and police again in the capital’s Mirpur area on Monday morning, as police moved to disperse workers attempting to gather on the roads.
At around 9:15am, police chased away workers who had taken positions on the road. As of the latest reports, confrontations between the two sides were continuing.
Hafizur Rahman, officer-in-charge of Mirpur police station, confirmed the incident, saying: “The workers came to block the road, and we dispersed them.”
Earlier on Sunday, garment workers clashed with police during protests demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000.
On Monday morning, when workers attempted to gather again in the Mirpur-10 area, police intervened, triggering a series of chases and counter-chases. Workers threw bricks and stones at police, who responded by firing tear gas shells.
The workers were subsequently dispersed, but tension remained high across the area. Most shops remained closed, while police restricted people from gathering on the streets and questioned individuals they considered suspicious.

item.title: Garment workers block Dhaka-Tangail highway again, traffic halted
item.description:
Garment workers blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway in Gazipur again on Monday, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000 and bringing traffic to a standstill.
The blockade began around 8:30am, when workers from several factories gathered on the highway in the Palli Bidyut area.
Mohammad Amjad Hossain, superintendent of Gazipur Industrial Police, said around 1,000 workers occupied the highway at the time, halting traffic in both directions.
He said Industrial Police and other law enforcement agencies were working to bring the situation under control and restore traffic movement.
On Sunday, workers staged protests in Konabari, Safipur, Palli Bidyut and surrounding industrial areas, demanding the same wage increase.
Workers and police clashed intermittently, escalating tensions at several locations. Protesters also set fire to a police box and vandalized several vehicles.
The unrest disrupted traffic on the Dhaka-Tangail highway for around six hours on Sunday.

item.title: 10 BGB platoons deployed in Gazipur, 21 magistrates assigned
item.description:
Ten platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) have been deployed in Gazipur to maintain law and order amid ongoing garment workers’ protests demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000. They are being assisted by 21 executive magistrates.
Arif Hossain, assistant commissioner of the Media and Research Cell at the Gazipur deputy commissioner’s office, confirmed the deployment in a message sent to the “Media Cell DC of Gazipur” group at 8:26am on Monday.
Sources at the deputy commissioner’s office and Industrial Police said Industrial Police, district police, BGB personnel and executive magistrates were working together to keep the situation under control.
Amjad Hossain, superintendent of Gazipur Industrial Police, said around 1,500 workers gathered in the Palli Bidyut area along the Dhaka-Tangail highway at around 8:30am on Monday, bringing traffic to a standstill.
BGB personnel, Industrial Police and other law enforcement agencies have been deployed in Chandra, Palli Bidyut, Safipur, Konabari and Mouchak to manage the situation and restore traffic movement, he added.
Garment workers in Gazipur have been protesting for the past two days, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000. Thousands of workers have occupied the highway at different points, halting traffic and causing severe inconvenience to long-distance bus passengers and other commuters.
The protests initially involved road blockades in Mouchak, Safipur and the Chandra-Palli Bidyut areas of Kaliakair, bringing traffic on the Dhaka-Tangail highway to a complete halt.
During the unrest, gates of several factories in the Palli Bidyut area of Kaliakair were vandalized. A police box was also vandalized in Mouchak, another was set on fire beneath the Konabari flyover, and a pickup van was torched in front of the Ansar Academy.
The unrest later spread to nearby industrial areas, including Ratanpur, Konabari and Kashimpur. Operations at around 30 factories in these areas were suspended amid the protests.

item.title: Clashes break out between garment workers, police in Ashulia
item.description:
Clashes broke out between garment workers and police in Ashulia, Savar, on Monday, prompting police to fire several rounds of tear gas shells to disperse the protesters.
No casualties were immediately reported. Following the clashes, workers and police remained in a standoff.
The incident occurred after 10am in the Narsinghapur and Nishchintapur areas along the Abdullahpur-Baipail road. Most factories along the road declared a general holiday amid the unrest.
According to witnesses, workers initially gathered in front of a factory owned by Ananta Group before moving to a Hamim Group factory, where they allegedly threw bricks.
Tensions escalated when the workers attempted to block the road to press home their demands, triggering a confrontation with law enforcement personnel and subsequent clashes.
Police fired several rounds of tear gas shells in an effort to disperse the workers and bring the situation under control.
Shoeb Ahmed, additional superintendent of police (operations and intelligence) at Industrial Police-1, said police were working to restore order.
A tense situation prevailed in the area at the time of filing this report, with additional police personnel deployed to maintain law and order.

item.title: I’m not GPA-5
item.description:
The publication of the Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examination results brings an unavoidable wave of introspection.
With the overall pass rate plunging to 52.12% -- a steep decline of 6.71 percentage points from the previous year, and the number of GPA-5 achievers dropping drastically-- the numbers tell an unvarnished story.
Across the nine general education boards, over five lakh students have failed, and institutions recording a zero-pass rate have multiplied.
While the immediate emotional fallout across households is palpable, this statistical correction is far more than a one-off examination anomaly.
It is the long-overdue collision between romanticized grade inflation and ground-level academic reality.
Beneath the surface, these figures expose a systemic crisis rooted in years of compound learning loss, structural distractions, and the alarming erosion of critical thinking skills-- a trajectory that threatens to cascade into tertiary education and further saturate an already overburdened job market.
To understand how we arrived at this juncture, we must trace back to the tectonic shifts triggered by the Covid-19 pandemic.
What began as emergency remote learning mutated into a permanent cultural shift in how students engage with technology.
Years of post-pandemic device dependency have fundamentally rewired adolescent attention spans.
Smartphones, initially embraced as digital lifelines for continuity of education, have morphed into engines of distraction.
Instead of functioning as portals for academic exploration, devices have become conduits for endless scrolling, short-form video loops, and digital escapism.
This hyper-engagement has manifested as severe, accumulated learning loss.
Cognitive reserves that ought to be dedicated to mastering complex calculus, scientific theories, or linguistic nuances are instead fragmented by algorithmic distractions.
Compounding this digital drift has been a profound sociopolitical redirection.
Over recent years, a significant segment of the student demographic found its primary locus of engagement not in classrooms, libraries, or laboratories, but in digital political activism, social media movements, and polarized public discourse.
While civic awareness is vital, the displacement of core academic commitment by unbridled digital mobilization hollowed out foundational learning.
Classrooms emptied of physical presence or mental focus, and textbooks were replaced by timelines and comment sections.
Consequently, foundational competency withered away, setting the stage for the widespread academic setbacks mirrored in the recent board results.
The direct casualty of this attention deficit is the erosion of creative and analytical capability.
For years, the education system leaned heavily toward rote memorization, rewarding students who could regurgitate predictable formulas rather than solve novel problems.
As learning loss compounded, even that mechanical proficiency broke down.
When faced with standardized assessments that demand critical thinking and conceptual synthesis, students trained on bite-sized digital content floundered.
They lacked the cognitive endurance to parse complex problems, construct logical arguments, or formulate creative solutions.
This manifested starkly in the examination halls, resulting in massive failures across English, ICT, and core academic subjects.
This erosion of creativity creates a dangerous pipeline into tertiary education.
Universities, already grappling with resource constraints and bloated classrooms, are forced to absorb cohorts of students who lack the bedrock skills for higher-tier research and specialized learning.
Instead of dynamic hubs of innovation, undergraduate institutions risk turning into holding pens for underprepared minds, churning out graduates who possess degrees on paper but lack the depth, adaptability, or intellectual curiosity required to navigate a complex modern economy.
The ramifications of this educational shortfall will inevitably bleed into the national job market, intensifying an already critical crisis of youth unemployment and underemployment.
Bangladesh’s economy faces an acute paradox: Industries routinely complain about a severe shortage of skilled, competent professionals, while thousands of university graduates remain unemployed or underemployed.
The influx of mediocre graduates from these compromised cohorts will only exacerbate this burden.
A degree stripped of genuine skill acquisition is nothing more than an expensive piece of paper.
Employers in corporate sectors, tech industries, and manufacturing are increasingly looking for value addition-- critical thinking, problem-solving agility, cross-functional technical skills, and robust soft skills such as communication, emotional intelligence, and adaptability.
Students whose formative high school and university years were compromised by digital distraction and superficial engagement graduate without these crucial competencies.
Unprepared for the rigour of the real world, they enter a saturated job market ill-equipped to set themselves apart.
The result is a swelling pool of frustrated, credentialed youth trapped in a cycle of joblessness, further straining socioeconomic stability.
Yet, within this sobering statistical downturn lies a silver lining of monumental proportions.
For too long, Bangladesh’s education policy was held hostage by a toxic obsession with inflating pass rates and distributing GPA-5s like confetti, creating a false sense of security while actual competency plummeted.
The government’s refusal to artificially cushion the HSC 2026 results marks a courageous departure from past populist optics.
By allowing the true picture to surface-- grounded in more rigorous, standardized evaluation metrics-- the administration has demonstrated a commendable, full-frontal focus on educational integrity.
Stopping the artificial inflation of grades is the first necessary step toward national self-reckoning.
This unvarnished reality check must not be viewed merely as a failure of students, but as a clarion call for systemic structural reform.
Let this moment serve as the definitive foundation-setting exercise for a long-term, multi-year master plan to revive education quality from the ground up.
Reviving our educational ecosystem requires a multi-pronged approach:
The drop in pass rates is a bitter pill, but it is the precise medicine our academic ecosystem requires.
By confronting these hard truths today, we lay the groundwork for a resilient, highly skilled generation tomorrow-- turning a temporary statistical dip into the catalyst for a permanent educational renaissance.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: An unsavoury tug of war
item.description:
As the self-declared return date of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina draws closer, discussion of the Awami League in Bangladesh’s political arena keeps growing. The party that those in power have declared “irrelevant,” is the very party they have now started a tug of war over.
On one side, BNP alleges that Jamaat-e-Islami is striking an understanding with them. On the other, Jamaat counter-alleges that BNP is scheming to bring the Awami League back into politics.
Although the Awami League was excluded from the February general election, the field stayed heated with discussion about whom its supporters would vote for, why they would vote for them, or whether they would vote at all. That discussion continues even after the voting. BNP leaders like to say that Awami League supporters voted for Jamaat.
The latest chapter of pointing fingers at each other was started by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman himself at a public rally in Rajshahi last month. “There is clear intelligence information that the autocrat who fled is supplying money there. Whom are they helping by supplying this money? There are some people, a party, who spread confusion in the country. Who tried to sell various tickets to the public before the election, telling lies. These two sides have become one.”
‘Autocrat’ and ‘ticket seller’
Needless to say, by “autocrat” the PM meant the Awami League, and by the party that “sold tickets” before the election, he meant Jamaat-e-Islami. Jamaat not only rejected this allegation but also made a counter-allegation that BNP came to power by striking an understanding with the Awami League. It is worth mentioning here, though, that even though eight months of the BNP government has passed, no result of this alleged understanding with the Awami League is yet visible.
Both parties claim to be the torchbearers of the 2024 anti-government movement, and day in and day out, they pledge to resist the Awami League’s return to politics. But from their recent talk, it appears that a large part of their politics is taken up by the party that was ousted in 2024.
Awami League leaders are saying that they will not cooperate with any party, whether BNP, Jamaat, or NCP. They want to convey that the ideological gap between the Awami League and these parties is so great that there is no question of an understanding among them.
On the other hand, in the backdrop of Bangladesh’s politics, the possibility of an “understanding” between the Awami League and either Jamaat or BNP cannot be ruled out entirely. A glance at the past shows that just as Jamaat has adopted various kinds of strategies to survive, in exactly the same way, the two big parties have used Jamaat to hurt each other.
It is often understood that Jamaat was rehabilitated in independent Bangladesh with the cooperation of General Ziaur Rahman and his party, BNP. But later the Awami League too did not hesitate to cooperate with Jamaat.
For example, in the 1986 election, the League and Jamaat participated when the other anti-Ershad parties, including BNP, boycotted the vote. The two parties conducted their anti-Ershad movement in coordination with Jamaat, although they refrained from giving Jamaat a place on their own platform. In the country’s politics there was still something called a sense of shame ( chokkhulojja ) then.
Jamaat in Khaleda’s cabinet
Jamaat’s relationship with BNP began to grow close after Ershad’s fall. Although BNP contested the 1991 election alone, many suspected at that time that an unwritten “understanding” had been reached with Jamaat. Although the BNP won the election, it did not get the seats necessary to form a government. After Jamaat’s 18 MPs extended their support, BNP was able to form the government.
A decade after the first cabinet of Khaleda Zia, BNP and Jamaat formally formed an alliance and jointly took part in the 2001 election. By then the sense of shame of the eighties and nineties had bid farewell to the country.
Having won the election, two former commanders of the Al-Badr force, Motiur Rahman Nizami and Ali Ahsan Mohammad Mujahid, got places in Khaleda Zia’s new cabinet.
The Awami League too has worked together with Jamaat to put BNP in a difficult position. The biggest example of this is the 1994 incident in which the two parties resigned from parliament together, demanding elections under a caretaker government. The two parties conducted the anti-BNP movement together, although outside parliament they never came onto one stage. The Awami League’s sense of shame was still maintained then.
BNP’s relationship with Jamaat is deep. They have contested elections in one alliance and formed a government together. They have agitated together and carried out violence across the country, including arson ( jalao-pora , “burn and torch”).
The Awami League has cooperated with Jamaat at certain times for strategic reasons, but in elections or on the streets, the leaders and activists of these two parties were not seen together.
Now the question is: In the present backdrop of politics, how likely is an “understanding” between the Awami League and Jamaat?
Anti-Awami unity
The prime minister spoke of “intelligence” information. Through this statement, it became known that the intelligence agencies have again become active in the political arena, collecting information on opposition parties. But have the intelligence agencies really given this information? And if they have, did they supply correct information, or are they arranging their briefs to serve the government’s current agenda?
The prime minister did not present any evidence in support of his statement, but merely saying “intelligence has information” is also not enough. This is especially so since, from 2001 onward, only BNP’s name was being added to Jamaat’s.
After the 2024 change of power, in the absence of the Awami League, the Jamaat sees itself as BNP’s rival for power. BNP too is getting the chance to shoot fish in a barrel. Neither of these two parties wants the Awami League to return to politics. They do not want it in their own interests. Opposition to the Awami League holds these two parties together in a kind of unity.
Jamaat probably sees the announcement of Sheikh Hasina’s return as a sign of some understanding behind the scenes. Along with them, the young leaders of NCP have also become somewhat restless over the Awami League question.
The protests, including long marches, by Jamaat and NCP in various regions of the country, are being held for the implementation of the July Charter. It can be assumed that another aim of this program is to keep up pressure so that the government does not become lenient towards the Awami League.
Awami League’s challenge
The war of words between BNP and Jamaat-NCP is now at the stage of the boxing “shadow fight.” The two sides are circling each other but are not trying to land a blow. If an understanding with the Awami League were proven, it would amount to betrayal of 2024. But through this, they are once again proving how relevant the Awami League is in Bangladesh’s politics.
For the Awami League’s leaders, the biggest challenge now is to hold the party together and to lift the morale of leaders and activists. There are three most important goals before them now. First, how Sheikh Hasina’s return to the homeland can be made successful. Second, lifting the ban on the Awami League’s activities. And third, freeing their leaders and activists from jail and settling the cases filed against them.
Why would the Awami League make an understanding with Jamaat to achieve these goals? None of these goals seems achievable with Jamaat’s help. It is foolish even to think that Jamaat would help the Awami League achieve its goals.
But BNP may perhaps think, and the intelligence agencies may perhaps have fed that thinking, that the Awami League’s aim is to create anarchy in the country and put the government in danger by weakening Tarique Rahman’s hand and force him to become lenient towards the Awami League. But even there, the possibility of an Awami League-Jamaat understanding is slim.
The Awami League needs to reach an understanding with the government, because it is through this understanding that Sheikh Hasina’s return can become possible and safe. Likewise, it is through an understanding with the government that the path for the Awami League’s return to politics can be smoothed. In reaching an understanding with the government, mediation by some third force will be needed, since BNP and the Awami League have stopped even seeing each other’s faces.
Sabir Mustafa is the former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster. Views expressed are the author’s own.

item.title: Gold prices rise by Tk3,194 per bhori after two days
item.description:
The Bangladesh Jewellers Association (Bajus) has raised gold prices in the domestic market, just two days after announcing a reduction, citing an increase in the price of pure gold in the local market.
The new rates came into effect at 10am on Monday. Under the revised prices, 22-carat hallmarked gold costs Tk18,935 per gram, or Tk220,786 per bhori (11.664 grams), including VAT.
The decision was taken at a meeting of the Bajus Standing Committee on Pricing and Price Monitoring on Monday morning, chaired by its chairman, Dr Dewan Aminul Islam Shahin.
According to the new price list, 21-carat gold costs Tk18,085 per gram, or Tk210,871 per bhori. The price of 18-carat gold has been set at Tk15,535 per gram, or Tk181,128 per bhori.
Gold made using traditional methods now costs Tk12,690 per gram, or Tk147,932 per bhori.
On Saturday, Bajus reduced the price of 22-carat gold by Tk5,481 per bhori, bringing it to Tk217,592, including VAT. The revised rate also took effect at 10am that day.
With Monday’s increase, the price of 22-carat gold has risen by Tk3,194 per bhori from the previous rate.
Bajus has also announced new prices for silver ornaments. The price of 22-carat silver has been set at Tk300 per gram, including VAT. The rates for 21-carat and 18-carat silver are Tk290 and Tk250 per gram, respectively, while silver made using traditional methods costs Tk190 per gram.
Bajus said making charges would depend on the design and craftsmanship of the jewellery. As VAT is included in the fixed retail prices, it cannot be charged separately.
For exchanges of old gold jewellery, 12% of the value must be deducted, excluding making charges and the cost of stones. For the purchase of old jewellery, the deduction will be 18%. VAT cannot be deducted separately in either transaction.
The revised prices will remain in effect at jewellery shops across the country until further notice.

item.title: Filipino woman injured in Banani gas leak fire dies
item.description:
A 32-year-old Filipino woman who suffered severe burns in a fire caused by a gas leak in the capital’s Banani area has died while undergoing treatment.
Keistin Ver Bunag died at around 3:30am on Tuesday at the National Institute of Burn and Plastic Surgery.
She had suffered burns to 63% of her body, while her respiratory tract was also damaged by smoke or hot gases.
Dr Sultan Mahmud Shikdar, a resident surgeon (emergency) at the institute, said Keistin was admitted to its emergency department on October 28 after being referred from Continental Hospital.
According to preliminary information, she sustained the injuries at around 7am that day while attempting to light a gas stove.
Her condition remained critical following admission. Despite receiving treatment and close medical attention, she could not be saved, the doctor said.

item.title: Key players out as Aussies name white-ball squads for England
item.description:
A host of key players have been left out as Australia revealed their squads for upcoming home white-ball assignments against England.
The Aussies will take on England in eight white-ball fixtures (three ODIs and five T20Is) from 13 November, with experienced pacers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood all left out of Australia's squad as they prepare for upcoming ICC World Test Championship series against New Zealand and India.
Fellow pacer Nathan Ellis will miss the ODI component of the series that commences in Perth as he continues his recovery from a side strain he picked up against South Africa in September, with a host of fresh players included in the squads for the eight fixtures.
Former ICC Men's Under-19 Cricket World Cup stars Mahli Beardman and Oliver Peake are included in the 14-player ODI squad alongside young all-rounders Jack Edwards and Liam Scott, while Nikhil Chaudhary and Joel Davies, Lachlan Shaw and Sam Harper are among the fresh faces in the T20I squad for the series that will follow.
Test stars Travis Head, Matthew Renshaw, Cameron Green, Alex Carey, Josh Inglis and Cooper Connolly will all skip the T20I component of the England fixtures after they feature in the ODIs, leaving plenty of new faces in contention to take on Australia's oldest rival.
"These ODI and T20 matches provide several players, many of whom have had opportunities on recent tours, with a great chance to further demonstrate their ability against very strong opposition," Australia selection chair George Bailey said.
"Liam Scott returns to the ODI squad and we are excited by the fact he learns from each opportunity and have seen him grow his game on the back of strong performances over the past 12-18 months. "Mahli Beardman's recent performances for Australia A were impressive and we are incredibly excited for his return to the national team across the ODI and T20 formats. We think he can continue to develop into an all-format player across the coming years.
"Lachie Shaw is a highly talented cricketer we also think will develop quickly and has a powerful game that will impact in the T20 format.
"Sam Harper has performed strongly in domestic cricket. He is in a great place with his game right now and is executing his style of cricket consistently, across all formats.
"Jake (Fraser-McGurk) and Mitch (Owen) return to the T20 side and we believe their ball-striking can be a point of difference in the shorter formats.
"They are good examples of players who have had an opportunity at the International level and have continued working on their game from what they learnt from those experiences."
Australia ODI squad: Mitchell Marsh (c), Xavier Bartlett, Mahli Beardman, Alex Carey, Cooper Connolly, Jack Edwards, Cameron Green, Travis Head, Josh Inglis, Spencer Johnson, Ollie Peake, Matthew Renshaw, Liam Scott, Adam Zampa

item.title: New Zealand lose key duo for home ODI series against India
item.description:
New Zealand have suffered a major blow with news that Mark Chapman and Rachin Ravindra will miss the upcoming five-match ODI series against India.
Chapman is still recovering from his hamstring injury and will require a further two weeks on the sidelines, while Ravindra is battling a shoulder problem and the Black Caps have decided the all-rounder requires further recovery time ahead of the two-match ICC World Test Championship series with India that commences later this month.
The absence of the duo will see batter-keeper Tim Seifert available for all five matches of the ODI series, while Henry Nicholls (games 1-3) and Dean Foxcroft (games 4-5) have been added to the squad.
New Zealand coach Rob Walter said it was a big loss to lose Chapman and Ravindra, but still feels his side is well placed to cope in their absence.
“Everyone knows what an asset Mark and Rachin are to this side so it’s a shame they have to miss this series,” said Walter.
“I caught up with Mark last week and although he’s disappointed he’s working hard to get back on the field.
“With Rachin, his shoulder hasn’t quite recovered to a position where he could field comfortably in white-ball cricket, so with the Test series later this month we don’t want to take any undue risks.
“We’re pleased to bring in Henry who is no stranger to this side, and Dean who recently featured in the ODIs against the West Indies."

New Zealand squad (games 4 and 5): Mitchell Santner (c), Finn Allen, Michael Bracewell, Kristian Clarke, Jacob Duffy, Matt Fisher, Dean Foxcroft, Lockie Ferguson, Mitch Hay, Nick Kelly, Tim Seifert, Blair Tickner, Will Young
