Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Monday that the threat of cyberattacks was growing due to the rise of artificial intelligence, adding that Moscow was taking “appropriate measures.”
He did not say who Russia believed was behind the incident.

item.title: Limited French school protests resume as holidays end
item.description:
French students returning from autumn holidays blocked some high schools on Monday, determined to reinvigorate a protest movement despite government concessions during the break.
Just one percent of France’s 3,700 high schools for 15 to 18-year-olds called lycées were blockaded, the education ministry said.
Pupils maintained their protest after hundreds of thousands of people, including students, took to the streets across France on Saturday for a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations.
The cost-of-living rallies emerged after high school students launched nationwide demonstrations in September over learning conditions and inequality.
The government has announced measures, including changing the university admissions process, ensuring more teachers and capping the number of pupils per class.
But some students say it is not enough.
In the southern city of Marseille, several garbage bins were stacked in front of the entrance to one high school on Monday morning.
“We’ve resumed the movement because we were supposedly given answers, but... it’s clearly not enough,” 16-year-old Meriem told AFP, perched on one of the dumpsters.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray told the France Inter radio station students should return to the classroom to avoid failing exams.
“I have students who are sitting the baccalaureate at the end of the year, and several hundred thousand of them haven’t attended classes for four or five weeks,” he said.
President Emmanuel Macron has called for classes to resume in a calm manner, arguing that “young people have been heard.”
With the European Union’s second-largest economy on the brink of recession and under pressure to rein in debt, the government has limited scope to appease student protesters through additional spending.

item.title: Mirpur police vehicle arson: Rashed Khan demands Jamaat chief’s arrest
item.description:
Prime Minister’s Political Assistant Rashed Khan on Monday demanded the arrest of Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami Ameer Dr Shafiqur Rahman, accusing him of instigating the arson attack on a police vehicle in Mirpur amid the garment workers’ demonstrations over wages.
“A police vehicle was set on fire in Mirpur. The Jamaat ameer should be arrested and brought to justice for this act of arson. As an instigator, he cannot evade responsibility for the incident,” Rashed said.
He made the demand while talking to reporters after a programme at the Jatiya Press Club.
Rashed alleged that Shafiqur had recently said if the people stood with Jamaat, the party would implement its seven-point demand and “smash everything of the government”.
“Awami League is hatching conspiracies, and Jamaat is behind these conspiracies. The party is instigating them. So, I believe the Jamaat ameer should be arrested over this arson attack and legal action should be taken against him,” the PM’s political assistant said.
Referring to the Jamaat ameer’s remarks at a recent long march and a subsequent Facebook post, he questioned the call for the government to take a tough stance.
“You said at the long march that everything would be smashed. Now you have posted on Facebook that the government must be tough. When you made that remark at the long march, did you not think about this?” Rashed asked.
He further alleged that the Jamaat chief could not evade responsibility for the alleged acts of anarchy, arson and violence being carried out by the “Awami League” across the country.
Meanwhile, garment workers continued demonstrations and blocked highways and major roads in Gazipur, Savar and Narayanganj on Monday, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000.
At least two vehicles, including a police vehicle, were set on fire in Gazipur and Savar, while a Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) member and an Industrial Police officer were injured in clashes with workers.
The unrest continued despite the government's formation of a six-member minimum wage board on Sunday to review the wage structure for garment workers amid widespread protests in the country's industrial belts.

item.title: Milon: Education has no gender
item.description:
Education Minister Dr ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon on Monday said education has no gender, questioning whether anyone in the world has ever said that people of a particular gender cannot receive education.
“Does education have any gender? Has anyone ever said that people of a particular gender can study while others cannot? I believe education has no gender,” he said.
The minister made the remarks while speaking as the chief guest at the certificate distribution and closing ceremony of the 210th Basic Training Course at the National Academy for Educational Management (NAEM) in Dhanmondi.
Referring to criticism over his earlier remarks on gender, Milon said a particular online newspaper had accused him of believing in transgender identity.
He said he had been discussing the representation of different gender identities in education and had cited data showing that the proportion of transgender people among those who qualified was less than one percent in that event.
The minister criticised what he described as the tendency of some media outlets to distort speakers' remarks and divert their intended meaning without listening to the full context.
“People should listen and understand before making comments. Creating panic in this way is very detrimental,” he said, urging the media to highlight positive developments alongside negative issues.
Speaking about the results of the SSC and HSC examinations, Milon said the country's education system had suffered a setback since the Covid-19 pandemic.
He said the practice of passing students without proper assessment had gradually weakened academic standards. He also referred to the impact of political developments and what he described as a growing tendency among students to become involved in politics instead of concentrating on their studies.
The minister said the BNP government is working to improve students' learning and writing skills, adding that weaknesses in higher education also needed attention.
Milon stressed the need for proper training and orientation for teachers, saying that unlike other cadres of the Bangladesh Civil Service, education cadre officers generally join their jobs without undergoing a structured training programme beforehand.
He said administrative cadre officers receive training after joining the service, while members of the armed forces and police also undergo professional training before taking up their responsibilities.
“Training makes people better. But teachers do not have that kind of training arrangement,” he said.
The minister said the government wanted to introduce a merit-based approach in training programmes, giving priority to those who perform well in presentations, classroom activities and assessments.
He said the basic training course needed to be made more comprehensive, as teaching models, modules and pedagogical approaches were gradually changing.
He said the government is considering how to make the best use of resources allocated to education.
The minister said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman had allocated the highest amount to the education sector, while the ministry was also working to ensure that the available resources were used effectively.
“We are working to build a future Bangladesh. The Prime Minister is working relentlessly towards that goal, and I have been given responsibility for this ministry to contribute to that effort,” he said.
He called upon everyone involved in education to think critically and analyse how the country's education system could be developed. “The collective thinking of all of us will be the driving force behind building the future Bangladesh,” he added.
Professor Prem Rizvi, Director (Training and Implementation) of NAEM, course adviser and convener of its Central Evaluation Committee, was also present at the event.
The programme was chaired by NAEM Director General Professor Dr Wasim Md Mezbahul Haque.

item.title: Salahuddin urges universities to lead in building technology-driven, merit-based society
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed on Monday called upon the country's universities to play a leading role in building a technology-driven, merit- and knowledge-based society to meet the challenges of the 21st century and achieve the vision of a modern Bangladesh.
The minister stressed the need to go beyond conventional education and focus on technological knowledge, innovation and intellectual development.
He made the call while addressing a discussion meeting as the chief guest at the central auditorium of Jagannath University (JnU) in Dhaka today, marking the university's 21st founding anniversary.
He urged universities across the country to promote innovative research, modern information technology practices and merit-based education.
Emphasizing continuity in public welfare initiatives, Salahuddin said that development-oriented activities should continue despite political changes in the country.
"Bangladesh first, people first" should be the guiding principle, he said, adding that a country is not merely defined by its territory or flag but also by the people's rights, ownership and participation.
Recalling the history of Jagannath University, the minister said that efforts to transform the institution into a university began in 1995 through the initiatives of Shaheed student leader Nasiruddin Pintu and others, alongside the commitment of former Prime Minister Begum Khaleda Zia.
Subsequently, in 2005, during the BNP government's tenure, an act was passed in Parliament to upgrade Jagannath University College into a full-fledged university.
He also mentioned that construction of a separate modern campus with residential facilities on 200 acres of land in Keraniganj is underway.
He assured students that the government maintains a positive attitude towards addressing their reasonable demands.
On higher education, the minister said that academic certificates and GPA-5 results alone cannot ensure national development.
Qualitative improvements in education and a stronger focus on research are essential, he stated.
He noted that universities should not function merely as institutions for preparing graduates for employment but should also serve as centers of intellectual freedom, advanced research, and knowledge creation.
Highlighting the importance of technical and vocational education, he urged students to develop practical skills and professional expertise in line with the demands of the modern world rather than pursuing conventional academic degrees without adequate employment opportunities.
Referring to the growing importance of the semiconductor industry, artificial intelligence (AI), and technology-driven economies, the minister said that innovative ideas, technological knowledge and a skilled workforce are indispensable for Bangladesh to remain competitive in the future.

item.title: 14 teachers, one student – and the only examinee fails
item.description:
A college in Muksudpur upazila of Gopalganj, with 14 teachers but only one HSC examinee this year, has recorded a zero pass rate after its sole candidate failed the examination.
Durbashur Adarsha Secondary School and College was among the institutions under the Dhaka Education Board where no students passed the Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) examination, results of which were published on Saturday.
According to college sources, only one student enrolled in the 2025-26 academic session and appeared in this year's HSC examination. The student failed, leaving the institution with a zero pass rate.
The result has sparked criticism among local residents, who blamed the institution's management committee, principal and teachers for its poor academic performance.
Local residents Balaram Ojha, Nirmal Biswas and Shubhendu Sarkar said students were reluctant to enroll because the institution lacked a proper learning environment.
They questioned how the college could continue operating in such a condition and suggested that its college section be shut down.
Established in 1988, the institution initially operated as a secondary school. Its college section was introduced in 2009, offering science, humanities and business studies.
All 14 teachers are enrolled under the government's Monthly Pay Order (MPO) scheme and receive regular salaries and allowances. The same teachers have also been conducting classes for the college section.
However, only the humanities group had an examinee this year, while the science and business studies groups had no enrolled students.
Principal Swarna Rani Biswas said the institution struggled to attract students because of its rural location.
"Students are hard to find as the college is in a village. Teachers also do not come regularly or show much interest in enrolling students. I have been trying to improve the situation and spending money from my own pocket every year, but nothing has worked," she said.
Founder Paritosh Sarkar said several teachers had left after failing to secure MPO benefits for the college section.
"The college section is not doing well. There is a shortage of both teachers and students. It would be better if it were closed," he said.
Governing body Chairman Parimal Kirtan said he had received his appointment letter only a week earlier and had yet to visit the institution or hold a meeting.
"I do not know much about these issues," he said.
Upazila Secondary Education Officer Mahfuza Begum said her office was responsible for supervising secondary-level education, not the college section. She said the Dhaka regional office was responsible for overseeing the college section.
Muksudpur Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Mahmud Ashik Kabir said he was aware that only one student had appeared in the HSC examination from the institution and failed.
"We will investigate the matter," he said.

item.title: UIU collaborates on Robo Fest 2026 in Jamalpur
item.description:
A day-long robotics festival, Robo Fest 2026, was held in Jamalpur on Sunday to introduce students to robotics, artificial intelligence and emerging technologies through interactive exhibitions and hands-on learning.
Organized by the Science and Innovation Club of United Public School & College, Jamalpur, and United Trust, in collaboration with United International University (UIU), the festival was held under the theme “A Journey into the World of Robotics”.
The festival featured technological innovations and projects developed by UIU’s Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (CAIR), including the UIU Mars Rover, UIU Aerial Robotics, UIU Rescue Rover and UIU Mariner.
Students from United Public School & College, M A Rashid Memorial Academy and M A Gafur Memorial Academy in Jamalpur participated in the event.
CAIR members presented innovations across 3 major areas of robotics: ground, marine and aerial. The ground robotics segment featured the Mars Rover and Rescue Rover, while the marine segment showcased the UIU Mariner. The UIU Aerial Robotics team also demonstrated its technologies and activities.
Students and visitors had the opportunity to learn about the mechanisms and practical applications of the showcased projects.
The exhibition also highlighted UIU teams' achievements in international competitions. The UIU Mars Rover team secured third place globally and first place in Asia at the University Rover Challenge (URC) 2026, along with the “Best Autonomous System Recognition” award.
The achievement marked a milestone for Bangladesh and was recognized as a unique accomplishment in the 20-year history of rover competitions in Asia.
Meanwhile, the UIU Aerial Robotics team secured fourth place globally at the Student Unmanned Aerial Systems (SUAS) 2026 competition, becoming the first Bangladeshi team to participate in the event.
The festival aimed to develop students' innovative thinking, creativity and problem-solving skills while encouraging their interest in science and technology. It also provided opportunities to gain practical knowledge of robotics, programming, artificial intelligence and engineering design.
Through initiatives such as Robo Fest 2026, the organizers seek to encourage students in Jamalpur to explore emerging technologies and participate in national and international science, programming and robotics competitions.

item.title: Best time to eat chia seeds
item.description:
Many of us kick-start our day with chia seeds. In contact with water, they take on a jelly-like form, which helps increase the feeling of fullness in the stomach and keeps you feeling full for longer. However, you can get their nutritional benefits not only in the morning but at any time of the day.
You can eat chia seeds mixed with yogurt, smoothies, oats, fruit, or pudding. They can also be added to soups, salads, and pancakes. However, there is one thing you must keep in mind before eating them: do not eat dry chia seeds directly. They absorb water quickly and swell up, which carries a risk of getting stuck in the throat. So it is safest to eat them soaked in water or another liquid, or mixed with a moist food such as yogurt.

item.title: The secret to spotless, fresh-smelling kitchen towels
item.description:
While cooking, curry spills or oil and turmeric splatter inside the microwave. Kitchen towels are often the first thing people reach for to clean up such messes. However, regular use can cause grease and dirt to build up in the fabric, leaving stubborn stains and unpleasant odours.
If not cleaned properly, damp and dirty towels can also create an environment where germs thrive.
To deal with this problem, many people repeatedly boil their towels in hot water or use different cleaning products. However, excessive heat or improper washing methods can damage the fabric's colour and texture. Keeping kitchen towels clean therefore requires proper care.
Here are some simple ways to remove grease stains and unpleasant odours using common household ingredients.
When oil, gravy or other food spills onto a kitchen towel, it is best to clean it as soon as possible. Once a stain dries, it can become trapped in the fabric fibres, making it more difficult to remove.
First, gently blot away excess oil or food particles with a tissue. Then rinse the stained area with water. To remove grease stains, apply a small amount of dishwashing liquid and leave it for 10 to 15 minutes. Gently scrub the area before rinsing it thoroughly.
For turmeric or tomato stains, make a paste by mixing a little baking soda with water. Apply the paste to the stain, leave it for a while and then rinse. However, it is advisable to test the mixture on a small, hidden area first, especially when dealing with coloured or delicate fabrics.
Soaking kitchen towels before washing can help loosen dirt, especially if they have been used for a long time or have accumulated excessive grease. Take a container of warm water suitable for the fabric and mix in detergent according to the product instructions. Soak the towels for some time, adjusting the duration according to the fabric type and level of dirt.
Baking soda can also help reduce unpleasant odours and assist with cleaning in certain cases. For removing stains from white fabrics, check the product instructions and fabric care guidelines before using hydrogen peroxide. It may cause coloured fabrics to fade. Always follow safety instructions before combining any cleaning products.
Kitchen towels usually come into contact with grease, food residue and different types of dirt. Therefore, it is better to wash them separately from everyday clothing.
Use water at the temperature recommended on the fabric care label, along with a suitable detergent. Although cotton towels can generally withstand relatively high temperatures, not all fabrics are suitable for washing in boiling water.
After washing, make sure no soap or detergent residue remains on the towels. This helps keep the fabric clean and prevents discomfort during use.
If kitchen towels still smell unpleasant after washing, they may need more thorough cleaning and proper drying. In some cases, white vinegar can help reduce unwanted odours. However, it is not a substitute for detergent. Before using it, check whether it is suitable for the fabric and follow the product instructions.
Caution: Never mix vinegar with bleach or other cleaning products, as this can trigger harmful chemical reactions.
Completely drying kitchen towels after washing is essential. Whenever possible, hang them outdoors or in direct sunlight. Leaving damp towels folded or in a moist environment for extended periods can cause unpleasant odours to develop.
After each use, hang towels in a place with good air circulation. Avoid using the same towel for too long and replace it regularly as needed.
Developing simple habits such as changing kitchen towels regularly, washing them separately from other clothes, and ensuring they are completely dry can make it easier to maintain cleanliness. These practices help reduce grease stains and unpleasant odours while keeping the kitchen more hygienic.

item.title: SRK’s new song released from his upcoming movie ‘King’
item.description:
Bollywood actor Shah Rukh Khan marked his 61st birthday on Monday with the release of “Tu Mil Jaaye”, the first song from his upcoming film “King”.
Released at midnight, the track features Shah Rukh Khan and Deepika Padukone, with Arijit Singh providing the vocals and Ed Sheeran performing an English rap.
The music video features a mix of romantic scenes, dance sequences, and action shots. It opens with Shah Rukh introducing his character through the dialogue: “Main qaatil nahi, aashiq hoon, aur nishana meri mashooka, aur woh aashiq hi kya jo dil cheer na de.”
Shah Rukh and Deepika are seen together in several locations, including a beach and a cafe. The video also features Shah Rukh in action sequences and a shirtless appearance. He is seen lip-syncing to Ed Sheeran's rap, while the closing dialogue offers a glimpse of the darker side of his character.
The film's cast also includes Suhana Khan, Abhishek Bachchan, Rani Mukerji, Anil Kapoor, Jackie Shroff, Jaideep Ahlawat, Arshad Warsi, Raghav Juyal, and Abhay Verma.
“King” is scheduled for a worldwide theatrical release on December 24, 2026.

item.title: Performance of a lifetime
item.description:
Theatre is often reduced to performance. An actor memorizes lines, puts on a costume, and inhabits a life long enough to make it convincing. We tend to assume that is what makes it theatrical: the act of becoming someone else. But performance is only one part of it.
A theatre also has a director, a script, critics, rehearsals, and an audience. It is, in essence, an institution built around visibility. Nothing in it means much until someone is there to witness it.
Femininity works the same way.
Not merely as performance, but as an existence continually arranged around spectatorship.
I felt it countless times. I felt that before I had words for it.
I was in a theatre with my family, waiting for the lights to go down, knees apart, when my mother leaned over.
“Girls don’t sit like that,” she said, gently.
She wasn’t angry. The correction came wrapped in concern. I knew what she meant: close my knees and take up less space. So, I did.
The play hadn’t even started, and I had already been reviewed.
We talk about femininity as something a woman simply has, a natural pull towards softness and grace, as if it grew out of the body unprompted. But nobody walks onto a stage already knowing the script. A girl learns hers through correction.
Sometimes from her close ones, sometimes from strangers. She learns which emotions make her too much and which make her agreeable. Her anger is unbecoming, but her empathy must be limitless.
She is told that her confidence is only admirable to a certain extent; that must stop once it begins to resemble authority. She is taught that beauty is rewarded not because it reveals character, but because it reassures an audience.
Over time they pile up, and one day the rehearsal stops feeling like a rehearsal. It feels like instinct.
That is ideology’s best trick: repetition passes for nature.
But performance alone cannot sustain theater. It requires an audience.
It needs someone to watch the fall.
The audience never needs to say a word. The actress fixes her posture because she knows she’s being watched. She hears the applause before it comes and the criticism before it’s spoken.
Girls learn this in the doorway, before they’ve entered any room.
Is my orna in the right place? Is my hair okay? Is this too much blush?
Checking what their bodies might be saying about them.
Under a watchful gaze, femininity does not bloom--it shrivels. The gaze arrives long before the observer. And at one stage, it no longer matters whether anyone has stayed to watch--the eyes, they’ve turned inwards.
Feminism named this long before it had language sophisticated enough to describe it: surveillance, prolonged enough, becomes self-surveillance.
The critic never leaves the theatre; he leaves his gaze in his old seat. And that is enough.
Maybe that’s why debates about femininity so often collapse into the question of choice, mistaking the structure for the performance. The interesting question is not whether the actress enjoys her costume, but whether she chose the stage at all.
Agency and structure are not opposites. A woman can be soft, kind, and forgiving. She can love dresses and flowers and lipstick, and none of it makes her smaller.
Those pleasures are real, even if they live inside a culture that rewards them.
Expectation doesn’t cancel out desire, and desire doesn’t make expectation disappear.
Both can be true at once. The two can coexist.
That is where femininity is most often misunderstood. Feminism isn’t suspicious of it because it is artificial.
Everything human is constructed to some extent:Language, law, nations. That doesn’t make any of it less significant.
What feminism questions is not the performance but the conditions under which it becomes compulsory. A role stops being expressive the moment leaving it is punished.
Perhaps that is what separates theatre from captivity.
In a theatre, the curtain always falls.
The actor takes off the costume, the audience goes home, and the role stays behind on the stage where it belongs.
Femininity has never given women that. It follows them off the stage and into mirrors, classrooms, relationships, every photograph ever taken, every family dinner ever sat through.
The stage follows them home, then one day it becomes home.
That’s why it can be exhausting even when you love it, even when you chose it. Not because it’s fake, but because there is no intermission.
I have a niece who is one. She can’t walk yet, and she has no opinion about colours. I wanted to buy her a doll, and I was scrolling through gifts marked “for
girls” before I even noticed. Then I stopped.
When did I start looking in this aisle? Why not a ball? A toy car? Why was I already steering her world towards pink?
Maybe feminism’s most radical move was never to tear down the theatre. Maybe it was to imagine a world where the actress can walk off the stage and still be recognized as herself.
Until then, the script keeps travelling, not through villains but through the people who love us. And through us.
Shuchi Binte Shahjalal is a writer who writes gently, honestly, and just a little dangerously about love and home.

item.title: The brown woman’s dilemma
item.description:
Award acceptance speeches often open with the recipient’s gratitude for one person: their mother. It is fitting. Mothers are where everything we know begins. They are the life-givers, the most tangible evidence we have of a creator. And for many of us, mothers shape our lives from beginning to end.
My mother’s stories were etched into every hall I grew up in.
From New York to Lusaka to Dhaka to Hanoi to Seoul to Port Moresby, and in the many homes and hotel rooms between, there were countless halls. Where my mother’s boundless insight fell short, I hounded the doors of the only other sages I knew: my aunts, my grandmothers, my sisters, and at times even my female teachers.
The more I sought, the more their insight felt like a confirmation of my responsibility to live for them.
Only now, older, do I see how little these women were allowed to live.
Lately, I am fascinated by bounds: boundaries, binding, and the shapes we form when we bind.
I have filled tens of books and notebooks between 2010 and 2026, most of them spiral-bound. The spiral weaves from hole to hole and tightens, tracing a circle that repeats the same shape but, funnily enough, never ends up quite where it began.
Around 2013, in a Dubai shopping mall, my father spotted a bright pink book with etchings of a mermaid, flowers, and butterflies adorning the cover.It was called Girls’ Miscellany: Fascinating Information Every Girl Should Know.He asked me if I wanted it.
“Oh, no, Baba,”
I shook my head, because that was how my mother usually responded to generous offers. It’s a habit I still have today.
To be a woman and directly ask for what you want remains unsettling to me. Really, I wanted that book. I liked books, mermaids, flowers, butterflies, and hot pink. I was intrigued by the large, unfamiliar word in the title.
At my denial, my father shook his head at the cashier.
“She doesn’t want it.”
What?
He wasn’t playing the game right.
“Wait. I changed my mind!”
I carried that book around with me for so long that its spine came loose. Pages grew thin and stained. I had memorized everything “miscellaneous” about its contents, including the long and dismal list of Henry Tudor’s wives--victims of his frustration at his own failure to bear a son.
And the fact that for centuries, women in ancient Chinese tradition were coerced into binding their feet and violently constricting the natural growth of their bones to gain a daintier appearance. It was called foot binding. “Pretty”, as a replacement for autonomy. “Woman”, as a replacement for “human”.
Boundaries are something I learned about in therapy. I was first brought to therapy when I was too young to understand what it was. In New York City, my mother would enter a large hall with mahogany wall-to-ceiling doors that slowly swung shut.
The doors swallowed her for about an hour while I played computer games with a friendly man outside.
I thought I was accompanying my mom while she spoke to lawyers about the mean things my Baba was doing.
Really, she was consulting lawyers regarding his pitiful crimes, both legal and moral, while her daughter spoke to a child therapist.
Eleven years later, therapists told me that boundaries were what healthy people used to avoid carrying the pain their mothers had endured at the hands of fathers, sons, misogynistic bosses, and so on.
Part of me distrusted this idea.
Before anything else, I am my mother’s daughter. What kind of living comes at the cost of betrayal?
A boundary seemed akin to shutting the doors to the years of love, sacrifice, good humor, and good grief that bound me to my mother.
Bangladeshi women know well that womanhood often strings up and binds women in hereditary ways.
I feel the pressures and pains my aunt, sisters, and mother have had to live through because, unfortunately, patriarchy is crafted of things far tougher than plastic.
This inherited baggage lives off the idea that self- sacrifice is a virtue.
The pains I inherited from living through women who don’t live caused me to idolize martyrdom.
As someone so connected to bounds, boundaries are still new to me. Boundaries don’t feel like they were made for someone like me, someone who is a woman and is Brown.But the older I get, the more I’m having to accept being self-defining in my identity. More and more, angering others feels like the price I have to pay for living.
Selfishness is a “crime”, and yet the self is all I have.
Is the selfish Brown Woman, then, nothing at all?
Deya Nurani is a freelance contributor based in the US.

item.title: Police detain several over unrest in Savar, Ashulia
item.description:
Police have detained several people from different areas of Savar and Ashulia over allegations of vandalism, attacks on garment factories and attempts to create unrest amid ongoing workers’ protests, Dhaka District Police Superintendent Shamima Pervin said on Monday.
However, she could not immediately confirm the number of people detained, saying arrests had been made separately by industrial police and police from Ashulia and Savar police stations.
Speaking to journalists in front of a factory in Jamgora on the Ashulia-Baipail road in the afternoon, Shamima said those accused of trying to vandalise vehicles, attack garment factories, injure workers and hurl brickbats had been detained.
She said police teams were still conducting operations and that the total number of arrests would be confirmed after information from different units was compiled in the evening.
Dhaka Range Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Md Mostafizur Rahman, who was also present during the visit, said the police would take strict legal action against those creating instability in the industrial belt and those backing them.
He said the government had formed a wage board for garment workers on Sunday and that it had already started its work to address wage-related concerns through the legal process.
“Those who are creating instability despite the formation of the wage board are not, in our view, part of the workers’ movement. They are people creating disorder in society, and strict legal action will be taken against them,” he said.
The DIG urged workers to return to their jobs without fear and called on factory owners to resume normal operations, assuring them that police would ensure security at factories.
He said police were collecting information about those allegedly instigating the unrest from behind the scenes, adding that no one would be allowed to act outside the law. Those involved in vandalism and arson at factories and other locations were being identified, and cases and arrests were underway, he added.
Addressing rumours that a worker had been killed by police gunfire, Mostafizur said no such incident had occurred and accused a group of spreading misinformation on social media to destabilise the country and mislead workers.
He urged journalists to report verified information, saying false claims could create confusion among workers and the public. He also warned that legal action would be taken against anyone spreading misleading information or inciting unrest, including labour leaders or others providing financial support.
The DIG said police had been monitoring several social media groups for the past four days, alleging that they were circulating provocative messages announcing demonstrations at specific locations for the following day.
He also expressed concern over the safety of students during the unrest, saying a student was injured by bricks thrown by protesters while trying to flee near a school at the Bangladesh Krira Shikkha Protishthan (BKSP) on Monday.
Mostafizur said a large number of police personnel had been deployed across the industrial belt, including uniformed and plainclothes officers, members of the Armed Police Battalion (APBn) and the RRF.
He said workers in some factories had initially entered their workplaces before gradually stopping work. After general leave was declared at the factories, they took to the streets to protest.

Two Mirpur metro stations reopen after nearly an hour
item.description:
Garment workers blocked roads in Mirpur for the third consecutive day today, Tuesday, demanding higher wages. Clashes broke out between workers and police in the morning. As a result, trains stopped calling at Mirpur-10 and Mirpur-11 metro stations.

However, metro services continued between Uttara and Motijheel, with passengers able to board and get off normally at all other stations.

Garment workers clash with police in Mirpur

Dhaka Mass Transit Company Limited (DMTCL), the agency responsible for building and operating the Dhaka metro rail, said trains stopped calling at Mirpur-10 and Mirpur-11 stations at 11:50 am.

All entrances to the two stations were closed for security reasons, preventing passengers from entering. As trains did not stop there, no passengers could get off either. Services resumed normal operations at around 12:30 pm, after the situation returned to normal.

A little after 10:00 am, garment workers took to the streets again. Clashes with police broke out at one point.

3 metro stations in Mirpur closed for hours amid garment workers’ protests

Protesters set fire to discarded wood and bamboo beneath Mirpur-11 metro station, bringing traffic on the road below to a halt. The metro rail stations were subsequently closed as well.

DMTCL sources said the metro rail police had advised the company to keep the two stations closed as a precautionary measure.

Last Sunday, Kazipara, Mirpur-10 and Pallabi metro rail stations were also kept closed for more than two hours. DMTCL describes this as “skipping” stations. This means train services continue to operate, but passengers cannot board or disembark at the affected stations.

item.title: Akhtaruzzaman released from prison in airport disorder case
item.description:
Former Major Akhtaruzzaman has been released from prison, a month after his arrest.

He was released from Dhaka Central Jail in Keraniganj on Tuesday morning. Golam Faruk, senior jail superintendent of Dhaka Central Jail, confirmed the news.

Golam Faruk told Prothom Alo that Akhtaruzzaman was released at around 10:00 am. Members of his family and party activists received him at the prison gate.

Akhtaruzzaman secured his release in a case filed over allegations of creating disorder and obstructing government duties amid a shortage of luggage handling services and trolleys at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka.

On 2 October, the Detective Branch (DB) of Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) arrested Akhtaruzzaman from his residence in DOHS, Cantonment, in connection with the case.

Police filed the case against him at Airport police station on the night of 1 October over allegations of creating disorder and obstructing government duties amid the shortage of luggage handling facilities and trolleys at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka.

Following his arrest, police produced Akhtaruzzaman before a court, which granted a one-day remand.

After failing to secure bail from the lower court in the case, Akhtaruzzaman applied to the High Court. Following a hearing, the High Court granted him interim bail with a rule on Sunday.

The state then filed an application seeking a stay on his bail. On Monday, the Appellate Division's Chamber Court issued a “No Order” decision on the state's application. The court passed the order after disposing of the state's petition.

Akhtaruzzaman is from Katiadi in Kishoreganj. He was elected a member of parliament from the Kishoreganj-2 constituency as a BNP candidate in 1991 and 1996, securing consecutive victories.

He contested the controversial 11th parliamentary election from the constituency with the BNP's electoral symbol, the sheaf of paddy, but lost. He also contested the 2024 national election as an independent candidate but was defeated.

Akhtaruzzaman once served as president of Kishoreganj district BNP. On 20 February 2022, the BNP expelled him for the fifth time over allegations of involvement in activities that violated party discipline.

After his expulsion, he remained in the public spotlight at various times by commenting on contemporary issues on television talk shows and social media. Amid these developments, Akhtaruzzaman joined Jamaat-e-Islami on 13 December last year, ahead of the 13th parliamentary election.

item.title: PM opens two-day Solar Expo-2026
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman today, Tuesday opened the two-day Solar Expo-2026 at the Bangladesh-China Friendship International Conference Centre in Agargaon in the capital on this morning.

After inaugurating the expo with the theme "Utilise Every Inch of Rooftop, Increase Income through Solar Power", the Prime Minister visited different stalls at the exhibition.

Jointly organised, for the first time, by the Power Division, the Ministry of Power, Energy and Mineral Resources, and the Infrastructure Development Company Limited (IDCOL), the exhibition showcases modern solar power technologies, bringing together policymakers, government agencies, development partners, financial institutions, technology providers and entrepreneurs.

It also highlights key aspects of the renewable energy sector, including government incentives, environment-friendly technologies, tax and tariff benefits, green and climate financing, carbon credits, solar-powered irrigation, and training and skills development opportunities.

The event aims to support the implementation of the National Renewable Energy Development Strategy (2026-2030) and familiarise stakeholders with government policies and incentives for promoting solar power.

Chaired by Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Iqbal Hassan Mahmood Tuku, the event was also joined by State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Anindya Islam Amit, Finance Secretary Md Khairuzzaman Mozumder and Power Division Secretary Mirana Mahrukh.

Ministers, state ministers, members of parliament, secretaries and senior government officials from different ministries also attended the inaugural ceremony.

item.title: RMG industry keeps growing despite challenges, but Bangladesh lags behind on wages
item.description:
Bangladesh’s garment exports continue to grow despite one crisis after another. The sector is ahead of other industries not only in business growth but also in terms of government support.

However, Bangladesh lags behind competing countries in the minimum wages paid to garment workers. Struggling to meet rising living costs amid persistent high inflation, workers have taken to the streets demanding higher wages.

According to data updated last March by Sweden-based H&M Group, one of Bangladesh’s leading buyers of readymade garments, garment workers in all seven countries—China, Cambodia, Indonesia, Vietnam, Pakistan, India and Turkey—receive higher minimum wages than workers in Bangladesh. The minimum wages in four other sectors in Bangladesh—tanneries, shipbreaking, sawmills and construction—are also higher than those in the garment industry.

In the face of workers’ protests, the Ministry of Labour formed a new wage board last Sunday. Protests have nevertheless continued in various industrial areas. Labour leaders say the unrest could have been avoided if the wage board had been formed earlier and the process of setting new wages had begun in time.

Factory owners, on the other hand, argue that workers’ wages are relatively low because of their lower productivity, the low prices of garments and narrow profit margins in garment manufacturing.

The current minimum wage for garment workers is Tk 12,500. The new wage structure came into effect on 1 December 2023. Previously, wage boards were formed every five years. The current BNP government has amended the labour law, reducing the interval for wage revisions to three years. Accordingly, the new wage structure must come into effect from December this year.

Asked for comment, Taslima Akhter, president of Garment Workers’ Solidarity, told Prothom Alo that rising prices of essential goods had made workers’ lives unbearable. They were being forced to cut food expenses.

Not only that, borrowing to meet household costs has also become more common. Workers had taken to the streets because they had reached the end of their tether, she said.

Garment exports on the rise

Bangladesh’s garment exports have grown despite at least seven major challenges over the past decade and a half. The fire at Tazreen Fashions in 2012 and the Rana Plaza collapse the following year caused a temporary downturn in garment exports. However, buyers’ confidence returned as work was undertaken to improve working conditions in garment factories. Exports also increased.

The garment industry subsequently faced a difficult period during the Covid-19 pandemic, but business recovered again. Over the past five years, the sector has sustained its exports despite the Russia-Ukraine war, political changes in the country, US reciprocal tariffs and the ongoing Middle East crisis.

Garment exports nearly doubled between 2011 and 2025. Last year, Bangladesh exported garments worth USD 38.82 billion, up 0.88 per cent from the previous year.

According to World Trade Organization (WTO) data published last July, China had the largest share of the global garment export market last year, at 27.5 per cent. Bangladesh ranked second, with a 6.76 per cent share. Vietnam accounted for 6.53 per cent, India 3 per cent and Turkey 2.3 per cent.

Tk 60 billion in tax concessions

For more than three decades, entrepreneurs in the garment industry have enjoyed various tax benefits. Citing the need to maintain their competitiveness in the global market, factory owners continue to receive tax concessions worth several billions of taka every year.

According to the latest report of the National Board of Revenue (NBR), the garment and textile sectors received corporate tax concessions worth Tk 58.29 billion in fiscal year 2022–23. This is because the garment sector has the lowest corporate tax rate among businesses, at just 12 per cent.

For environmentally friendly factories, the rate is only 10 per cent. Companies in other sectors, however, have to pay corporate tax ranging from 20 to 45 per cent.

Besides income tax concessions, the garment industry also receives cash incentives for exports to various markets. Factory owners also enjoy bonded warehouse facilities.

Under this arrangement, garment manufacturers do not have to pay customs duties or taxes on raw materials such as yarn, fabric and other goods imported from abroad. Only a handful of other sectors, including the leather industry, enjoy bonded warehouse facilities. Other sectors do not receive these benefits.

Wages lower than in competing countries

When the minimum wage of Tk 12,500 came into effect in the garment industry in December 2023, the exchange rate was Tk 110.50 to the US dollar. At that rate, the minimum wage was equivalent to USD 113. Over the past three years, the price of the dollar has risen to Tk 124. This means the minimum wage is now equivalent to USD 101.

According to H&M Group’s data from last March, however, the minimum wage for garment workers in Bangladesh is USD 102. In neighbouring India, it is USD 124. The figures for other countries are USD 294 in China, USD 208 in Cambodia, USD 172 in Indonesia, USD 163 in Vietnam and USD 135 in Pakistan.

Asked why wages are lower, Mohammad Hatem, president of the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA), told Prothom Alo, "Unlike competing countries, Bangladesh has the position of helper in the garment industry. Even people with no work experience can be recruited to this position at Tk 12,500."

"Machine operators earn Tk 18,000 a month without overtime. Experienced workers earn as much as Tk 25,000. Besides, our workers are less productive than those in other countries. The comparatively low wages are also due to the fact that we produce low-priced garments and earn less from cutting and making (CM)," he added.

Cost of living has increased

Although wages in the garment industry were raised three years ago, workers have not benefited because of high inflation. Inflation rose to nearly 9.75 per cent in fiscal year 2023–24. After the government changed in August following the uprising led by students and the public, workers launched a movement demanding higher wages. In response to the movement, workers received a nine per cent annual increment in January last year, instead of five per cent.

Inflation stood at ten per cent in fiscal year 2024–25. It declined somewhat to 8.68 per cent in the outgoing fiscal year. Until last September, wage growth had remained below inflation for 56 consecutive months. After the ongoing Middle East crisis intensified, fuel price increases pushed up the prices of essential goods once again.

A survey by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), published last month, found that average monthly household expenditure was highest in city corporation areas, at Tk 46,778. The figure was Tk 37,344 for urban households and Tk 32,532 for rural households. At the national level, half of household expenditure goes towards food and the other half towards non-food items.

Asked for comment, Khondaker Golam Moazzem, president of the research organisation Knowledge Hub Institute Trust, told Prothom Alo, "Eleven factors are considered when setting the minimum wage, including the cost of living, inflation, wages in competing countries and productivity."

"Taking these factors into account, we said three years ago that the minimum wage needed to be Tk 17,500 to meet workers’ living costs. Given the high inflation now, there is scope for a substantial increase in wages,” he added.

Khondaker Golam Moazzem also believes that, alongside food and medical allowances, education, transport and recreation allowances should be introduced.

item.title: Garment workers clash with police in Mirpur
item.description:
Garment workers took to the streets again today, Tuesday to stage protests in Mirpur, the capital. Clashes broke out between the workers and police.

At around 10:30 am, the workers gathered beneath the Mirpur-11 metro station and began protesting there. At one point, they threw bricks and stones at police from three directions.

Police fired sound grenades and tear gas shells to bring the situation under control. The two sides also engaged in chases and counter-chases.

Garment workers block highway in Gazipur, 50 factories declare holiday

Police beat several workers with batons.

The workers gathered wooden furniture on the road, set it on fire and staged protests. The incident created a tense situation in and around Mirpur-11.

Eyewitnesses said police officers were positioned on the western side of the Mirpur-11 metro station. Meanwhile, groups of workers arrived from Mirpur-10, various lanes in the Nanna Market area and Mirpur-12 to join the protest. At one point, they threw bricks and stones at police from three directions.

The workers also gathered wooden items, including benches, on the road and set them on fire as part of their protest. To bring the situation under control, police officers fired sound grenades and tear gas shells. They also chased the workers in an attempt to disperse them.

Garment workers have been protesting for several days, demanding that the minimum monthly wage be raised to Tk 30,000. On Saturday and Sunday, workers blocked roads in various areas, including Mirpur-10, Mirpur-11 and Mirpur-12.

How much should garment workers actually be paid?

On Sunday, clashes broke out between workers and police in the Mirpur-10 area, involving chases and counter-chases and the exchange of brickbats. At one point, a police vehicle was set on fire beneath the Mirpur-11 metro station.

Police said several people had been arrested from different locations in connection with the incident.

Workers also tried to take to the streets at various points in Mirpur on Monday, but police stopped them. Tear gas shells were fired at several locations. Today, workers have once again taken to the streets in Mirpur to stage protests.

item.title: Garment workers block highway in Gazipur, 50 factories declare holiday
item.description:
Garment workers blocked the Dhaka–Tangail highway in Gazipur and staged protests at around 9:30 am today, Tuesday, demanding that the minimum wage be raised to Tk 30,000. Protests by workers were reported in various parts of the district as well.

At around 9:30 am, workers took up positions on the Dhaka–Tangail highway in the Naojor area of Gazipur city. Many of them were seen carrying sticks. This brought traffic to a halt on that section of the highway, leaving passengers on long-distance buses and other vehicles stranded.

Garment workers clash with police in Mirpur

To avoid any untoward incidents amid the workers’ protests, the authorities declared a holiday today at 50 garment factories in various parts of the district. As a result, workers at these factories could not report for duty.

According to industrial police and local sources, at around 9:30 am, workers from Panasia Limited came out of their factory in the Naojor area of the city and took up positions on the western side of the highway flyover.

They then blocked the highway by putting up bamboo barricades. Traffic came to a halt on both sides of the highway. At the same time, workers from several factories in the Konabari, Mouchak and Telichala areas also stopped working and took to the streets.

Earlier, at around 9:45 am on Monday, workers had taken up positions on the highway in Naojor and staged protests by setting fires. Traffic was brought to a halt. During the protests that day, several police vehicles were set on fire. Workers also took to the streets and staged protests at various locations in the Konabari and Mouchak areas of the city.

No reports of road blockades like those seen in previous days came from the Chandra and Palli Bidyut areas of Kaliakair today. However, the situation there remained tense.

Amid the workers’ movement, members of law enforcement agencies were seen on alert at key points along various roads in the industrial area. Leaders and activists of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) and its affiliated organisations also took up positions at several points.

How much should garment workers actually be paid?

Gazipur Industrial Police Superintendent Amzad Hossain said efforts were under way to persuade workers in the Naojor area to leave the road. He said protests by workers were continuing in some areas today as well. Law enforcement personnel were present in Naojor and were trying to persuade the workers to clear the road.

For several days, various industrial areas in Gazipur have witnessed protests, road blockades, vandalism and arson over the demand for a minimum wage of Tk 30,000. Several people, including police officers and journalists, have been injured in these incidents. Police vehicles, other vehicles and factory warehouses have also been set on fire.

item.title: Americans vote in midterms set to upend Trump presidency
item.description:
Americans deliver their verdict on Donald Trump's tumultuous second presidency Tuesday in midterm elections that threaten to shatter his grip on Washington, with Democrats poised to seize the House and challenge for control of the Senate.

Republicans losing the House would give Democrats the power to stall Trump's legislative agenda and launch sweeping investigations of his administration. A Senate defeat would also threaten his ability to appoint Supreme Court justices and senior officials.

The election amounts to a nationwide judgment on Trump, with the mood turning sharply against Republicans amid anger over soaring living costs and the war against Iran.

All 435 House seats and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are at stake, along with governorships in 36 states. Democrats need only three House gains and a net four seats in the Senate to wrest both chambers from Republican hands.

Trump returned to office last year promising to bring down prices, but inflation, tariffs and fuel costs inflated by the Middle East conflict have squeezed Americans.

The 80-year-old's approval rating has hovered near the low 30s.

In the suburbs of Atlanta, Georgia, retired teacher Jane Callum, 77, was among Democrats canvassing for Senator Jon Ossoff who framed the race as a watershed moment for the country's future.

"I really feel an obligation to do everything that I possibly can to change the direction that our country is going in now, and put it more on the path to democracy and away from autocracy," she told AFP.

Democrats, Trump hold final rallies before midterm elections

Economic discontent

Republicans insist that Trump's tax cuts and immigration crackdown will benefit Americans and they are portraying Democratic candidates as left-wing radicals.

But in his final public campaign appearance Monday, Trump barely touched on the economy and spent most of the time in a rambling talk about his problem-plagued renovation of Washington's Reflecting Pool.

"This is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime," he said, 26 minutes into the speech, before quickly returning to talking about renovations.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer branded it a "pathetic closing message."

Some Republican supporters remain confident.

"We're going to win. As a matter of fact, we've probably already won," Texas military veteran Yvonne Clouser told AFP.

But while Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, the battlefield is extending into conservative states like Kansas, Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Alaska.

Democrats must also defend competitive seats, including in Michigan, where a bitter internal dispute saw congresswoman Haley Stevens endorse Republican Mike Rogers rather than the Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed.

Decision Desk HQ's final forecast forecasted 241 House seats for Democrats against 194 for Republicans, and a narrower 52-48 Democratic Senate majority.

US strikes Iran’s Qeshm Island ahead of midterm elections

Disputed results?

Polls can underestimate one party's support, and Republicans hope their voters turn out in force on Election Day.

More than 57 million Americans had already voted early before Tuesday, indicating the high energy.

The campaign has attracted more than USD 11 billion in political advertising, while billionaire Trump ally Elon Musk has poured hundreds of millions of dollars into Republican political efforts.

As soon as polls close, concerns will mount over whether results will be accepted by the Republicans.

Trump, who tried to overturn his 2020 election defeat, has repeatedly alleged widespread voter fraud and accused Democrats -- with no evidence -- of cheating.

The Justice Department, run by a close Trump ally, has already sued to potentially block certification of Alaska's Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan narrowly loses, although a court ruled against the effort on the eve of the election.

And the Supreme Court rejected on Monday an emergency bid to force California to set aside the mail-in ballots of more than 20,000 people on the grounds they may not be American citizens.

Trump, who will watch the midterms results at the White House on Tuesday night, signaled that if he does lose control of Congress he could simply defy Democrats.

"I veto everything," he told a podcast Monday, although he said he might strike deals with Democrats eventually.

item.title: US strikes Iran’s Qeshm Island ahead of midterm elections
item.description:
The United States on Monday attacked Iran's Qeshm Island, the Wall Street Journal reported, even as President Donald Trump signaled progress in negotiations with Tehran to end the eight-month-old conflict.

The Journal, citing unnamed US officials, described the strike against Qeshm, the the largest island in the Strait of Hormuz, as the latest of a series of limited strikes Washington has secretly carried out against Iran in recent weeks.

Democrats, Trump hold final rallies before midterm elections

Iranian state news agency IRNA reported five explosions in rapid succession were heard on the island, and that some residents reported seeing two aircraft flying in its skies.

The Pentagon referred questions about the reported strikes to US Central Command, which did not immediately respond to an AFP request for comment late Monday.

The Journal reported that US has been engaged in smaller-scale strikes against Iran for several weeks.

The paper said the US has not publicly announced the attacks, so as not to signal any intention of resuming major combat operations.

It said some officials described the assaults as defensive in nature to prevent Iran from having the freedom to attack commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, a key conduit for oil shipments that has been largely blocked since the war began in late February.

Trump rules out new Iran attack before US midterm elections

On Monday, on the eve of midterm elections in the United States, Trump said that a deal with Tehran "could happen."

Oil prices, sent rocketing by Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz energy corridor, plunged by more than seven percent on Monday on optimism over a possible end to the conflict.

item.title: How much should garment workers actually be paid?
item.description:
Thousands of garment workers took to the streets. Clashes with police and incidents such as vehicles being set on fire unfolded within a short time. The workers are demanding a minimum wage of Tk 30,000.

Some have expressed irritation, asking whether workers have become too demanding—is Tk 30,000 something that can simply be handed out? Others want to know how reasonable the demand actually is.

The good news is that the government has announced the formation of a new wage board. However, there is a tendency to look for government conspiracies in everything, whether right or wrong. This time has been no exception.

The minimum wage was set at Tk 12,500 in December 2023. Since then, the cost of living has risen significantly due to war, inflation, gas shortages and other factors. According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics, inflation stood at 8.34 per cent in September 2026.

The wage growth rate was 8.05 per cent in August. In this way, inflation has consistently outpaced wage growth for nearly four and a half years since February 2022. In other words, the real income of working people has declined every month for the past four and a half years.

RMG workers clash with police in Ashulia amid protests, vehicle set on fire, 2 detained
If we use minimum fairness as the benchmark, the worker’s wage should be at least Tk 17,500 simply to maintain the previous level of real income—that is, to adjust for inflation. Second, to keep the shortfall from exceeding the previous Tk 3,000, the wage would need to be Tk 18,000.

Expenses have increased by 16.7 per cent, while wages have risen by 6.7 per cent. For every Tk 1 increase in wages, expenses have gone up by Tk 3. Where will the additional money come from?

Drawing on my earlier research on garment workers, I recently set out to examine the situation on the ground and update my understanding of their circumstances. In the process, I gained a fairly clear picture of a garment worker’s monthly expenses. In January 2026, a family of four was living on the earnings of a single worker.

At an average of Tk 4,500 per person, the family needed Tk 18,000 to cover basic necessities—expenses that were essential for survival. There was no luxury, no new spending and certainly no savings. Including overtime, the worker earned a total of Tk 15,000. The remaining Tk 3,000 had to be borrowed; otherwise, the family had to survive on mashed potatoes and lentils for the last 10 to 15 days of the month.

RMG workers block Dhaka–Narayanganj link road

My calculations show that by January 2027, the minimum amount needed for the family to survive will be Tk 21,000, based on an average of Tk 5,250 per person. The worker’s earnings, including the wage increase and overtime, will be no more than Tk 16,000.

That leaves a shortfall of Tk 5,000. The figures may vary slightly, but over the course of a year, the worker’s monthly debt will increase by an additional Tk 2,000 on top of the existing Tk 3,000.

Meanwhile, because of the depreciation of the taka, the real value of the worker’s Tk 16,000 income in January 2027, calculated at January 2026 prices, will be only Tk 13,714. In other words, although the wage has technically “increased” on paper, real income has fallen by nearly Tk 1,286, or 8.6 per cent.

If we use minimum fairness as the benchmark, the worker’s wage should be at least Tk 17,500 simply to maintain the previous level of real income—that is, to adjust for inflation. Second, to keep the shortfall from exceeding the previous Tk 3,000, the wage would need to be Tk 18,000.

Dhaka-Tangail highway blocked again by garment workers, BGB deployed

This means that the government, or the owners through government mediation, must somehow provide an additional Tk 2,000 in assistance on top of the Tk 16,000 wage. Otherwise, how will the worker survive? Third, if there is a genuine willingness to eliminate the shortfall entirely, the worker must be paid at least Tk 21,000.

Note that the Tk 2,000 in assistance is not a bonus; it is the minimum condition for keeping the family in the same debt-ridden position as before. Otherwise, the family will slide from poverty into extreme poverty, struggling to afford even one or two meals a day.

British sociologist Seebohm Rowntree first demonstrated that a minimum wage could be measured against a budget covering a family’s basic needs. This tradition gave rise to Richard and Martha Anker’s “living wage” methodology, which is now an internationally accepted and widely recognised standard.

According to the Global Living Wage Coalition’s 2025 estimates, the living wage for a worker in Dhaka, supporting a family of four in which an average of 1.58 members earn an income, is Tk 30,459 per month. The workers’ demand for Tk 30,000 almost exactly matches the figure in this international research.

In his book Poverty and Famines, Amartya Sen showed that the Bengal famine of 1943 was not caused by a shortage of food. It happened because people’s “entitlements” collapsed: the amount of rice they could buy with their wages suddenly fell.

Two.

According to the ILO’s Minimum Wage Fixing Convention, 1970 (No. 131), the needs of workers and their families, as well as the cost of living, must be taken into account when setting minimum wages. Automatically adjusting wages in line with the cost of living is an established practice in many countries.

In his book Poverty and Famines, Amartya Sen showed that the Bengal famine of 1943 was not caused by a shortage of food. It happened because people’s “entitlements” collapsed: the amount of rice they could buy with their wages suddenly fell.

Rice was available in the market, but workers could no longer afford it with their wages. A garment worker’s entitlement is their wage. When the ratio between wages and the price of rice declines, deprivation enters the household even when the markets are full.

Economics also offers an answer to the concern that “factories will not be able to operate if wages are raised too much”. The “efficiency wage” theory developed by economists George Akerlof, Carl Shapiro and Joseph Stiglitz holds that better wages increase workers’ productivity, reduce employee turnover and save on training costs.

Government forms new wage board to increase garment workers’ salaries

Economists David Card and Alan Krueger showed in New Jersey, in the United States, that raising the minimum wage did not reduce employment. Card received the Nobel Prize in 2021 for research in this field.

The government and factory owners have one question: who will pay for this?

The responsibility does not rest with factory owners alone; all three parties have a role. International buyer brands have kept garment prices under control for years. It is the responsibility of the government and factory owners to persuade them to ensure that workers’ wage costs are separately protected in the purchase price. Factory owners must also allocate a fair share of their profits to wages.

The state, meanwhile, must arrange to cover part of the shortfall through rationing, subsidised essential goods, housing and transport assistance. Amartya Sen and Jean Drèze have called this “public action”. When the market cannot keep people alive, the state must take responsibility.

The concerns of factory owners are also valid. There are shortages of gas and electricity. Tensions in the Middle East have made the fuel market uncertain. Buyers do not want to raise prices. Competition with Vietnam and Cambodia is intense. If wages are suddenly doubled, smaller factories may shut down, putting workers at risk of losing their jobs and suffering further hardship.

In pictures: Police use tear gas, water cannons as garment workers clash in Mirpur

But if one reality is emphasised while another is ignored, disaster is inevitable. Real incomes have declined for four and a half consecutive years. The living wage under international standards is Tk 30,459, while the minimum wage has remained stuck at Tk 12,500 for nearly three years.

Workers taking to the streets are therefore not demanding extravagant benefits; they are seeking the minimum assurance needed to survive. Understanding this with empathy will point the way to a solution.

Of the country’s export earnings of USD 48 billion in fiscal year 2025–26, USD 38 billion, or approximately 80.6 per cent, came from the garment sector. Bangladesh is the world’s second-largest garment exporter after China.

The workforce taking to the streets is the very force behind the dollars needed for imports, foreign exchange reserves and the exchange rate. It is economically flawed and unjust to expect the families of those who generate 80 per cent of the country’s export earnings to survive on debt.

*Helal Mohiuddin is a faculty member in Liberal Arts at Mayville State University, North Dakota, USA.

*The views expressed are the author’s own.

item.title: Prothom Alo to celebrate anniversary tomorrow with a range of programmes
item.description:
Prothom Alo is preparing to celebrate its anniversary with a festive atmosphere and a range of activities. Preparations are under way for special supplements, a redesigned app, various programmes organised by the Bondhushava, and a reunion for employees.

The entire Prothom Alo family is busy making arrangements for the celebrations. Tomorrow, 4 November, marks the 28th anniversary of Prothom Alo.

The newspaper has taken several initiatives for its readers, well-wishers and employees to mark the occasion.

With the motto “ja kichu bhalo, tar shonge Prothom Alo (Prothom Alo stands with everything that is good)”, the newspaper published its first edition on 4 November 1998.

With its crisp printing, colourful photographs, 12-page format, new feature pages every day, commitment to political neutrality, practice of objective journalism, professional excellence and continuous efforts to embrace new ideas, Prothom Alo became an indispensable companion for the people of Bangladesh. It became a member of their families.

Within just a few years, Prothom Alo earned recognition as the country's most widely circulated daily newspaper.

Overcoming various challenges and adversities, it has evolved into more than just a newspaper, becoming a digital platform as well, while remaining committed to truth and facts. Beyond Bangladesh, Prothom Alo has received a warm welcome from Bengali-speaking readers around the world.

It has also earned prestigious recognition from international organisations such as WAN-IFRA and INMA, receiving awards as one of the world's and Asia's best media outlets.

To mark the anniversary, special supplements will accompany the main newspaper on four days.

The supplements, scheduled for publication on 4, 6, 8 and 10 November, will explore various aspects of the country's people and society, the relationship between citizens and the state, the perspectives of the younger generation, and questions and analyses concerning the future of Bangladesh.

Over these four days, the main newspaper and its supplements will together comprise 32 to 36 pages.

The special supplements will seek to explore a range of questions: what life is like for people in different parts of the country, whether in the capital, rural areas, river islands or the hills; what debates are taking place over the relationship between citizens and the state; where Gen Z finds meaning in life; and what Bangladesh's future might look like.

Prominent writers from across the country will contribute articles, while interviews with experts from various sectors will also feature. Details of the supplements have been published in an advertisement on the back page of today's Prothom Alo.

On 4 November, the anniversary itself, Prothom Alo will launch a redesigned version of its app. The updated app will introduce several new features to provide readers with an easier and more convenient experience. Its design and navigation system will also undergo changes.

As in previous years, Prothom Alo has organised a reunion for its employees to mark the anniversary. The event will take place at a venue in the capital on 4 November.

Prothom Alo representatives working in Dhaka and across the country will attend. Discussions at the event will cover the newspaper's future plans, new ideas and various aspects of the media industry.

Yesterday, Monday, the organisation held an online preparatory meeting involving employees from Dhaka and other parts of the country.

Prothom Alo Bondhushava has also arranged various programmes across the country to mark the anniversary. These include a range of public welfare and cultural activities. Through these initiatives, the organisation aims to strengthen its engagement with local communities.
